items.title: USN-9202-1: Kerberos vulnerabilities
items.summary: It was discovered that the Kerberos KDC incorrectly handled certain ASN.1 encodings in requests. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue to cause the KDC to crash, resulting in a denial of service. (CVE-2026-107364) It was discovered that the Kerberos KDC incorrectly handled malformed client names in PAC data during S4U2Proxy requests. A remote attacker controlling a trusted cross-realm KDC could possibly use this issue to cause the KDC to crash, resulting in a denial of service. This issue only affected Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and Ubuntu 26.04 LTS. (CVE-2026-107708) It was discovered that Kerberos incorrectly handled certain KRB-CRED messages. A remote authenticated attacker could possibly use this issue to cause services that accept forwarded credentials to crash, resulting in a denial of service. (CVE-2026-107778) It was discovered that the Kerberos password change service did not enforce the lockdown_keys principal attribute. An authenticated attacker with administrative privileges could possibly use this issue to bypass security restrictions and change the keys of a protected principal. (CVE-2026-107884) It was discovered that Kerberos incorrectly handled PAC server checksum verification. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue to bypass security restrictions. This issue only affected Ubuntu 26.04 LTS. (CVE-2026-111423) It was discovered that the Kerberos GSS-RPC client did not properly free memory when handling certain replies. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue to cause Kerberos client programs to consume excessive memory, leading to a denial of service. (CVE-2026-112314) It was discovered that the Kerberos GSS-RPC library did not properly free memory under certain circumstances. A remote attacker could possibly use these issues to cause the Kerberos administration server to consume excessive memory, leading to a denial of service. (CVE-2026-112315, CVE-2026-112316, CVE-2026-112320, CVE-2026-112321) It was discovered that Kerberos did not properly free decrypted key material when a post-decryption check failed. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue to cause the Kerberos KDC or administration server to consume excessive memory, leading to a denial of service. (CVE-2026-112317) It was discovered that the Kerberos administration server did not properly handle empty policy names. An authenticated attacker could possibly use this issue to cause the Kerberos administration server to crash, resulting in a denial of service. (CVE-2026-112318) It was discovered that the Kerberos GSS-RPC library did not enforce size limits when decoding data. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue to cause the Kerberos administration server to consume excessive resources, leading to a denial of service. (CVE-2026-112319) It was discovered that the legacy AUTH_GSSAPI authentication flavor in the Kerberos administration server lacked protections against resource exhaustion. A remote attacker could possibly use these issues to cause the Kerberos administration server to consume excessive resources, leading to a denial of service. This update disables AUTH_GSSAPI in the Kerberos administration server by default. It can be re-enabled by setting the GSSRPC_ALLOW_AUTH_GSSAPI environment variable for kadmind. (CVE-2026-112322, CVE-2026-112323) It was discovered that Kerberos did not properly verify RPCSEC_GSS call arguments. An attacker in a machine-in-the-middle position could possibly use this issue to alter the arguments sent by a legitimate client to RPC services, or cause return values to be sent in plain text. (CVE-2026-118380) It was discovered that Kerberos inefficiently decoded long ASN.1 sequences. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue to cause Kerberos to consume excessive CPU resources, leading to a denial of service. It was discovered that Kerberos did not properly free decrypted key material when a post-decryption check failed. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue to cause the Kerberos KDC or administration server to consume excessive memory, leading to a denial of service. ( CVE-2026-112317 )

It was discovered that the Kerberos administration server did not properly handle empty policy names. An authenticated attacker could possibly use this issue to cause the Kerberos administration server to crash, resulting in a denial of service. ( CVE-2026-112318 )

It was discovered that the Kerberos GSS-RPC library did not enforce size limits when decoding data. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue to cause the Kerberos administration server to consume excessive resources, leading to a denial of service. ( CVE-2026-112319 )

It was discovered that the legacy AUTH_GSSAPI authentication flavor in the Kerberos administration server lacked protections against resource exhaustion. A remote attacker could possibly use these issues to cause the Kerberos administration server to consume excessive resources, leading to a denial of service. This update disables AUTH_GSSAPI in the Kerberos administration server by default. It can be re-enabled by setting the GSSRPC_ALLOW_AUTH_GSSAPI environment variable for kadmind. ( CVE-2026-112322 , CVE-2026-112323 )

It was discovered that Kerberos did not properly verify RPCSEC_GSS call arguments. An attacker in a machine-in-the-middle position could possibly use this issue to alter the arguments sent by a legitimate client to RPC services, or cause return values to be sent in plain text. ( CVE-2026-118380 )

It was discovered that Kerberos inefficiently decoded long ASN.1 sequences. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue to cause Kerberos to consume excessive CPU resources, leading to a denial of service. ( CVE-2026-119079 )

Alejandro Pacheco discovered that Kerberos did not reject unkeyed checksums in CAMMAC verifiers. An authenticated attacker could possibly use this issue to bypass authentication indicator requirements. ( CVE-2026-71199 )

Erin Liman discovered that the Kerberos PKINIT module incorrectly handled certain CMS messages. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue to cause the KDC to crash, resulting in a denial of service. ( CVE-2026-71200 )

items.title: CVE-2026-134070 - Improper input sanitization in the AWS Config remediation runbook AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3
items.summary: Bulletin ID: 2026-203-AWS Publication Date: 11/25/2026 11:30 AM PST Description: AWS Systems Manager Automation provides AWS-managed runbooks that customers can run directly or through integrations such as AWS Config remediation. Session Manager, a capability of AWS Systems Manager, stores each account's regional session preferences in the SSM-SessionManagerRunShell document. We identified CVE-2026-134070, where improper input validation in the AWS-managed AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3 might allow an authenticated remote user who is permitted to run the runbook to set unintended configuration in the account's Regional Session Manager preferences document (SSM-SessionManagerRunShell) via a crafted S3KeyPrefix parameter value. This applies only when that document does not already exist in the Region. The unintended configuration can include arbitrary commands, which then run on managed instances when other users start Session Manager sessions. Impacted versions: Revisions created before 2026-10-22 (UTC) Refer to the article for the most up-to-date and complete information.
items.details:
Bulletin ID: 2026-203-AWS Scope: AWS Content Type: Important (requires attention) Publication Date: 11/25/2026 11:30 AM PST

AWS Systems Manager Automation provides AWS-managed runbooks that customers can run directly or through integrations such as AWS Config remediation. Session Manager, a capability of AWS Systems Manager, stores each account's regional session preferences in the SSM-SessionManagerRunShell document.

We identified CVE-2026-134070 , where improper input validation in the AWS-managed AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3 might allow an authenticated remote user who is permitted to run the runbook to set unintended configuration in the account's Regional Session Manager preferences document (SSM-SessionManagerRunShell) via a crafted S3KeyPrefix parameter value. This applies only when that document does not already exist in the Region. The unintended configuration can include arbitrary commands, which then run on managed instances when other users start Session Manager sessions.

Impacted versions: Revisions created before October 22, 2026 (UTC)

This issue has been addressed in a fixed revision of the AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3, available in all Regions where the runbook is available. The fixed revision is the latest revision in each Region. Its revision number varies by Region. To find it, run: aws ssm describe-document --name AWSConfigRemediation-EnableSystemsManagerSessionManagerAuditLogsToS3 --region <region> --query "Document.LatestVersion" We recommend upgrading to the latest revision and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes. Update any Automation executions, State Manager associations, AWS Config remediation configurations, or other automations pinned to an earlier revision to use the latest revision.

Any user permitted to run the runbook can choose which revision to run. Earlier revisions remain runnable until AWS deprecates all revisions created before October 22, 2026 (UTC), beginning January 15, 2027, in every Region and partition. Until then, follow the protection described under Workarounds, and confirm that all invocation paths use the latest revision.

The fixed runbook updates only the S3 bucket and prefix fields of an existing Session Manager preferences document, so any settings injected before you updated remain in place. You need to review a Region only if your Session Manager preferences document (SSM-SessionManagerRunShell) was first created there by an earlier revision of this runbook, not by you. To check: Look for any run of this runbook that failed with "DOCUMENT CREATE OR UPDATE FAILED." An injected run always fails with this error. Find when the document was first created by running aws ssm list-document-versions --name SSM-SessionManagerRunShell --region <region> and noting the CreatedDate of the first version. If that date matches a run of this runbook, the runbook created the document. To view the current settings, run aws ssm get-document --name SSM-SessionManagerRunShell --region <region> --query Content --output text. Repeat this check in each Region where you use Session Manager. Look for settings you did not configure, especially: shellProfile: commands that run at the start of every session, runAsEnabled and runAsDefaultUser: the operating system user that sessions run as, maxSessionDuration and idleSessionTimeout, the logging destination fields (s3BucketName, s3KeyPrefix, cloudWatchLogGroupName, kmsKeyId).

If you find any, restore your trusted preferences and review instances on which Session Manager sessions were started while those settings were active.

Until AWS removes earlier revisions in your Region, do one of the following:

Keep untrusted users from running earlier revisions of the runbook.

Keep a trusted Session Manager preferences document (SSM-SessionManagerRunShell) in every Region. Earlier revisions inject only when they create this document, so while a trusted one exists, this path is closed in that Region.

Keep this protection in place until earlier revisions are removed. Also complete the review described under "Review your Session Manager preferences".

We would like to thank k4ddy for collaborating on this issue through the coordinated vulnerability disclosure process.

Please email aws-security@amazon.com with any s ecurity questions or concerns.

items.title: Italy and Switzerland warn of autonomous AI-driven cyberattacks
items.summary: Swiss and Italian cybersecurity agencies are warning about automated cyberattacks powered by AI agents targeting organizations in the critical infrastructure sector. [...]
items.details:
Swiss and Italian cybersecurity agencies are warning about automated cyberattacks powered by AI agents targeting organizations in the critical infrastructure sector.

The two agencies listed four AI-powered penetration testing and red-teaming frameworks that have been involved in recent breaches and hacking incidents : ARTEX AI, CyberStrikeAI, DeepSeek Harness - Red Team, and PentAGI.

Both agencies have urged organizations to reduce the number of systems exposed on the internet, prioritize patching, and monitor for unusual activity.

CSIRT Italia says it detected large-scale malicious campaigns that used autonomous AI agents to identify and exploit vulnerabilities and misconfigurations on exposed endpoints.

In some cases, the agency observed multiple AI agents working in parallel to compromise a large number of systems within a few hours.

In one instance involving a DeepSeek Harness setup, a coordinator assigned tasks to five AI agents that undertook a broad spectrum of operational stages, from information gathering to exploitation and persistence.

The agents chained vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and compromised credentials, leveraging exposed systems as a foothold to reach internal networks.

“During the observed campaigns, autonomous agents demonstrated the ability to carry out complex, sustained activity to detect misconfigurations, link even low-impact vulnerabilities into complex attack chains, and dynamically adapt their operating modules,” CSIRT Italia says .

“They went as far as writing malicious code in real time to evade endpoint defenses and carry out actions deeper within the infrastructure.”

The Italian cybersecurity agency advises administrators to prioritize patching internet-facing systems, focus on addressing flaws known to be actively exploited in the wild, and disable remote management interfaces if not needed.

The agency also recommends monitoring control plane operations, authentication sources, traffic to internal networks, and outbound server traffic to detect suspicious activity.

Switzerland’s National Cyber Security Center (NCSC) warned of similar campaigns targeting organizations in the country, confirming the first cases of successful AI-assisted cyberattacks.

“In recent days, the NCSC has received its first reports of cyberattacks against organisations in Switzerland in which the attack was carried out with the assistance of an AI agent,” the Swiss NCSC said .

“Various organisations and operators of critical infrastructure across at least two sectors have been affected by these cyberattacks.”

“In all cyberattacks known to the NCSC, the use of AI agents led to the successful compromise of the victim’s IT systems.”

The agency described rapid attacks in which agents exploited weak passwords and known vulnerabilities in exposed endpoints, using frameworks to verify weaknesses and independently decide what to do next.

NCSC says that the number of AI agents publicly (and often freely) available to cybercriminals has nearly doubled since October, resulting in these massive waves against Swiss organizations, including critical infrastructure operators.

The agency recommends that administrators of internet-facing systems patch critical vulnerabilities within 24 hours of release, add multi-factor authentication (MFA) or passkey protection, and enforce least-privilege principles.

items.title: Oh, is it Thanksgiving? I hadn’t noticed!
items.summary: In true Thanksgiving fashion, David has a few thank-yous to give to the cybersecurity community (and a few choice words for threat actors).
items.details:
In true Thanksgiving fashion, David has a few thank-yous to give to the cybersecurity community (and a few choice words for threat actors).

Let’s start off with something I’m pretty sure none of us are thankful for: threat actors. Seriously, screw you guys! I know I'd be out of a job without you, but that’s just another way of saying “I coulda been a professional bagpiper.” There are days when that doesn’t sound so bad. So, no gratitude coming your way, people!

In terms of actual thankfulness, I want to give a big THANK YOU to the entire Blue Team, everywhere. Everyone out there defending, especially those in the U.S. taking shifts on Thursday to keep the turkey-eating public safe and secure. This is a hard, often high-pressure job for which you get little thanks, but all the blame when a breach occurs. We see you. We appreciate you. We promise we’ll save you some stuffing.

Speaking of defenders, I’m also very thankful to get to work with so many talented and wonderful people here at Talos. I’m not just saying this because I know my boss will read it! Without exception, everyone I’ve worked with here has not only been an expert at what they do, but they’ve been friendly, welcoming, and very patient with me as I’ve been feeling my way around this new org over the past several months. Thank you!

Finally, and maybe most importantly of all, I want to thank you , our readers. You are the reason we’re all here, doing what we do, helping you to look out for your own networks and protect your own people. We appreciate your trust!

Whether you’re celebrating Thanksgiving here in the States or just having a normal weekend wherever you are, I hope you get some time to relax, unplug, recharge, and de-stress.

In Talos’ latest blog , we examine the fascinating tradecraft of the OpenAI-linked agentic swarm that broke out of its containerized environment in 2026. While not inherently malicious, this swarm of AI agents used public internet services as improvised infrastructure to bypass their sandbox constraints and complete their training tasks. By analyzing this unintentional great escape, we can learn how multi-agent systems coordinate, partition work, and adapt when their paths are blocked. This view into autonomous AI operations provides a baseline for understanding how these behaviors transfer to purpose-built cyber attack frameworks.

The leap from an AI sandbox escape to weaponized cyber attacks has already happened. Agentic frameworks like ARTEX are currently in the wild, proving that multi-agent systems can move from a single compromised credential to deep network access in under 15 minutes. These autonomous threats adapt to errors in real time and execute dozens of actions in mere seconds. Understanding how these swarms coordinate, adapt, and exfiltrate data is a necessity to keep up with an adversary that operates at machine speed.

To catch an AI swarm, defenders must look for its operational fingerprints. Monitor your environment for irregular "burst-and-pause" timing patterns that indicate rapid, sub-second automated reasoning. Keep a close eye on unusual traffic to allow-listed public services like “webhook.site”, which agents use to park data before terminating. Finally, hunt for self-labeling conventions, like highly specific URL parameters or predictable file names (e.g., “artex-probe-*”), that agents rely on to track their state. Read the full blog for a deeper dive into these swarm behaviors.

AI-assisted cyber attacks trigger unauthorized payments at Indian banks and fintech firms The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) warned the attacks have resulted in unauthorized financial transactions at banking and financial services entities, as well as technology service providers supporting government-linked payments and platforms handling vendor or partner payouts. ( The Hacker News )

JPMorgan, Visa confirm customer data taken in third-party vendor hacks Marketing data, including email addresses, were affected. Both Visa and JPMorgan said the incidents were unrelated to tech disruptions reported earlier this week. ( Cybersecurity Dive )

OpenAI and Cisco unveil AI-assisted Linux security tool to block exploits before patching OpenAI and Cisco have teamed up to launch Shirudo (meaning "shield" in Japanese), an open-source Linux runtime that allows AI agents to defend systems without downtime. ( The Hacker News )

AI-enabled campaign targets Check Point Security Management servers The attacks led to at least 22 organizations being compromised across the globe, including in the UK, the U.S., France, Germany, Australia, China, India and Australia. The targeted organizations work in the energy, transportation, financial services and government sectors. ( Cybersecurity Dive )

Drupal Fail2Install exploit details emerge as critical RCE flaw faces active exploitation While Drupal has checks in place to determine whether the website is already installed before allowing installation to proceed, the research found that it's possible to bypass these checks by exhausting server resources. ( The Hacker News )

Beers with Talos: Ranksgiving with guest Anton Chuvakin This Ranksgiving, Dave has a brand new (though no less controversial) topic: the top five kitchen utensils/gadgets needed to make Thanksgiving dinner. Prepare to be both aghast and disappointed (as usual) in the team's choices.

UAT-12643 blends blockchain resilience with targeted infostealing Talos discovered UAT-12643 using Overlord RAT, which implements a command-and-control (C2) resilience technique in which encrypted server URLs are embedded in Solana blockchain transaction memos.

Securing Grandma's groceries with Pierre Cadieux Pierre takes us back to his early days on help desks in the 90s, where learning to correlate logs between Windows and Unix systems sparked the curiosity that eventually led him to security.

items.title: Rapid7 Named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Integrated Security Operations Center Systems
items.details:
We are proud to share that Rapid7 has been recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Integrated Security Operations Center Systems. The Gartner Magic Quadrant evaluates vendors based on their Ability to Execute and Completeness of Vision, and we are honored to be included among the recognized vendors in this important report.

Recognized for Completeness of Vision and Ability to Execute.

We are proud to share that Rapid7 has been recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Integrated Security Operations Center Systems.

Most security teams don't struggle to find tools. They struggle to make them work together. We believe SOC analysts lose too much of their day moving between consoles and matching alerts to assets by hand, which is time not spent stopping threats.

To us, an integrated approach to security operations means detection, investigation and response working from the same data and the same view, so analysts can get from "what fired?" to "what do we do about it?" faster.

Rapid7 Incident Command, part of the Rapid7 Command Platform, brings together SIEM, SOAR, DFIR, attack surface management and threat intelligence. We built it on the idea that exposure management, and the context it brings, belongs inside the SOC, not next to it. In our view, when an alert arrives with what we know about the asset and how exposed it is, analysts can prioritize what matters instead of working from separate vulnerability reports and alert queues.

We believe adopting an integrated SOC shouldn't be all-or-nothing. Incident Command is available in tiers from Essentials to Ultimate, so teams that want extra coverage can add managed services. That helps resource-pressured teams to start with what they need and grow at their own pace, spending less time building and maintaining integrations and more time on investigations.

To us, security operations work best when analysts have the context to act, not another console to check. We're proud to be recognized as a Leader in this Magic Quadrant, and we believe it reflects our focus on bringing detection, response and exposure context together for our customers. ⠀ The Gartner Magic Quadrant evaluates vendors based on their Ability to Execute and Completeness of Vision. We are honored to be included among the recognized vendors in this important report. Learn more about the Gartner Magic Quadrant here .

items.title: Cisco UCS and UCS-Based Appliances UEFI Shell Secure Boot Bypass Vulnerability
items.summary:
A vulnerability in the Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) Shell implementation of Cisco UCS Servers and UCS-based appliances could allow an authenticated attacker with valid credentials for a user account with the role of user or admin or an unauthenticated attacker with physical access to an affected device to bypass UEFI Secure Boot validation checks and execute unauthorized software. This vulnerability is due to the availability of memory write commands in the UEFI Shell while UEFI Secure Boot is enabled on a device. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by selecting the UEFI Shell boot option at boot time and using available shell commands to modify UEFI memory variables. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to manipulate the preboot environment, overwrite UEFI Secure Boot-related memory values, and execute unauthorized software on the affected device. Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability. This advisory is available at the following link: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-ucs-uefi-sb-bypass-eb6xC5GW
Security Impact Rating: High
CVE: CVE-2026-20293

A vulnerability in the Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) Shell implementation of Cisco UCS Servers and UCS-based appliances could allow an authenticated attacker with valid credentials for a user account with the role of user or admin or an unauthenticated attacker with physical access to an affected device to bypass UEFI Secure Boot validation checks and execute unauthorized software.

This vulnerability is due to the availability of memory write commands in the UEFI Shell while UEFI Secure Boot is enabled on a device. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by selecting the UEFI Shell boot option at boot time and using available shell commands to modify UEFI memory variables. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to manipulate the preboot environment, overwrite UEFI Secure Boot-related memory values, and execute unauthorized software on the affected device.

Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability.

This advisory is available at the following link: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-ucs-uefi-sb-bypass-eb6xC5GW

This vulnerability affects the following Cisco products if they have UEFI Secure Boot enabled and are running a vulnerable BIOS version:

5000 Series Enterprise Network Compute Systems (ENCS) ( CSCwu42927 )

Cisco appliances that are based on a preconfigured version of a Cisco UCS C-Series Server are also affected by this vulnerability if they support UEFI Secure Boot and expose access to the keyboard, video, and mouse (KVM) or virtual KVM console. At the time of publication, this included the following Cisco products:

Application Policy Infrastructure Controller (APIC) Servers

1. Physical KVM access is required to exploit the vulnerability on these appliances, which significantly reduces the attack vector on these platforms.

For information about which Cisco software releases are vulnerable, see the Fixed Software section of this advisory.

Only products listed in the Vulnerable Products section of this advisory are known to be affected by this vulnerability.

The UEFI Shell is a command line interface that provides commands to debug, script, and control various booting options. It is available as a boot option on Cisco UCS Servers that are in UEFI boot mode.

The UEFI Shell includes multiple commands that allow memory modifications. When UEFI Secure Boot is enabled on a device, the availability of such commands could allow an attacker to manipulate the preboot environment, including the possibility of overwriting UEFI Secure Boot-related memory values, effectively bypassing UEFI Secure Boot validations.

As a resolution for this vulnerability, UEFI Shell commands that allow memory modifications are removed from the shell when UEFI Secure Boot is enabled on a device.

There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability.

Cisco considers any workarounds and mitigations (if applicable) to be temporary solutions until an upgrade to a fixed software release is available. To remediate this vulnerability and avoid future exposure as described in this advisory, Cisco strongly recommends that customers upgrade to the fixed software indicated in this advisory.

In the following tables, the left column lists Cisco software releases. The right column indicates whether a release is affected by the vulnerability that is described in this advisory and the first release that includes the fix for this vulnerability. Customers are advised to upgrade to an appropriate fixed software release as indicated in this section.

Note: Upgrading Cisco Integrated Management Controller (IMC) and BIOS on Cisco 5000 Series ENCS requires upgrading Cisco Enterprise NFV Infrastructure Software (NFVIS) on the platforms. Cisco IMC and BIOS are upgraded as part of the firmware auto-upgrade process.

UCS B-Series M6 and X-Series Servers in UCS Manager Mode

UCS C-Series M5 Rack Servers in Standalone Mode or Intersight Managed Mode

UCS C-Series M6, M7, M8 Rack Servers in Standalone Mode or Intersight Managed Mode

UCS C-Series M6, M7, M8 Rack Servers in UCS Manager Mode

Note: For Cisco appliances that are based on a preconfigured version of a Cisco UCS C-Series Server, administrators can perform a direct upgrade of the Cisco IMC and BIOS software using one of the fixed releases mentioned in the preceding tables. For instructions, see the Cisco Host Upgrade Utility User Guide . The exceptions are the appliances that are listed in the following table. For these appliances, follow the instructions in the Remediation column:

The Cisco Product Security Incident Response Team (PSIRT) validates only the affected and fixed release information that is documented in this advisory.

The Cisco PSIRT is aware that proof-of-concept exploit code is available for the vulnerability described in this advisory.

The Cisco PSIRT is not aware of any malicious use of the vulnerability that is described in this advisory.

Cisco would like to thank Stas Lyakhov from Eclypsium for reporting this vulnerability.

To learn about Cisco security vulnerability disclosure policies and publications, see the Security Vulnerability Policy . This document also contains instructions for obtaining fixed software and receiving security vulnerability information from Cisco.

We are aware of CVE-2026-136267, an issue in Kiro Web where tool-call markup inside content an agent session read, such as a repository file or a web page, could be repeated by certain models and run as a command in the subscriber's hosted development environment without a consent prompt. items.title: CISA warns of critical unpatched flaw in Danfoss refrigeration controllers
items.summary: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) is warning about a critical vulnerability in Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series controllers used by food retailers to manage commercial refrigeration, HVAC, and lighting systems. [...]
items.details:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) is warning about a critical vulnerability in Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series controllers used by food retailers to manage commercial refrigeration, HVAC, and lighting systems.

Danfoss controllers have been compromised recently in attacks at various supermarkets and food retailers across Europe where hackers remotely shut down cooling systems or raised their temperatures.

The security issue is tracked as CVE-2026-129713 and received a severity score of 9.8. It is a stack-based buffer overflow in the controller’s server.

CISA says an attacker can trigger the flaw without authentication, cause the server to restart, and potentially achieve remote code execution with the web server's privileges.

Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA controllers are central control units for supermarket and convenience-store refrigeration. They are used to manage equipment such as refrigerated display cases and compressor racks, to log temperatures, and to alert when changes occur.

Danfoss calls the product line the AK-SM 800A Series, which includes the 820A, 850A, and 880A models. Depending on the model, they can also control store lighting and HVAC.

CISA notes that the controllers are deployed worldwide, but their exact number remains unclear.

On November 20, Danfoss published a security advisory saying that the CVE-2026-129713 vulnerability would be addressed in the upcoming software version 5.5.x for Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series.

The company said that the update would also remove the option that allows customers to turn off ‘Strict mode’ in the product.

Currently, there is no patch available for CVE-2026-129713, and potentially impacted system administrators are advised to take the following actions:

Keep controllers off of the public internet and minimize network exposure where possible.

Segregate control systems from business networks and place them behind firewalls.

Use up-to-date Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) when remote access is required.

Danfoss systems were recently targeted in high-impact cybersecurity incidents across Europe. Between October 11 and 12, several French supermarkets and food retailers suffered significant losses after attacks attributed to Iran’s IRGC-linked Shahid Kaveh unit compromised Danfoss AK-SM/AK-SC and Copeland/Dixell XWEB refrigeration controllers and remotely altered their defrost settings .

On November 2, at least 115 supermarket stores in Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden, Luxembourg, Ireland, Romania, and Estonia, had their refrigeration equipment shut down or their settings changed remotely .

Supplier Sabcobel said the attackers used the same vulnerability previously seen in the October attacks in France, indicating that Danfoss systems were involved again.

On the same day, attackers suspected to be linked to the same campaign targeted a refrigeration supplier for the French national blood service, altering cold-storage settings at three facilities.

items.title: More Pentests Without More Pentesters: Where AI Safely Helps
items.summary: Penetration testers spend a significant portion of their engagements on documentation, reporting, and other tasks outside of testing. PentestPad explains how AI can reduce this workload, help teams handle more engagements, and keep sensitive client data within their own infrastructure. [...]
items.details:
Penetration testers spend a significant portion of their engagements on documentation, reporting, and other tasks outside of testing. PentestPad explains how AI can reduce this workload, help teams handle more engagements, and keep sensitive client data within their own infrastructure.

Demand for penetration testing keeps rising, be it due to DORA threat-led testing, NIS2, or customer security questionnaires. However, supply often cannot keep up.

Experienced testers are scarce, take months to hire and train, and every one of them spends part of each engagement on work that is not testing. For a company that sells hours, that unbillable part is the margin.

This article shows how to measure it, which parts AI can take over, and how to do that without sending client vulnerabilities to someone else's servers.

Most companies track billable testing time and lack a number for the rest. If you tag the last ten engagements by phase, the picture usually changes:

Two ratios matter: documentation plus review as a share of testing time, and calendar days from last testing day to report delivery. The first sums up to the hidden cost, but only the second is what clients feel.

The tasks that suit a language model are the ones where the tester already knows the answer and needs it written down:

Drafting finding text from tester notes, using your own vulnerability library as the template, so tone and structure stay yours.

Normalizing and de-duplicating scanner output from Burp, Nessus, Nuclei and similar tools into one set of draft findings.

Consistency review: missing remediation, severity that does not match the CVSS vector, the same issue worded three ways.

Executive summary drafts, built from the validated findings and then edited.

It will be helpful to decide beforehand in what capacity to keep humans on severity decisions, exploit validation and anything the client will rely on as a statement of fact.

A model that confidently describes and is set to run an exploit chain that nobody verified can be is worse than no help.

PentestPad covers the whole engagement, from scoping and scanner imports to findings, client delivery and retests.

Its AI can run against a self-hosted LLM inside your own network.

Import scanner output and tester notes into one project as draft findings.

Pull in matching entries from your reusable vulnerability library.

Let the model rewrite each draft in your house style. The tester edits and approves.

Senior reviewer works through comments on the report itself, not email.

Export the branded report (DOCX or PDF) or deliver it through a client portal.

Track remediation and retest status on the same findings.

If an AI agent is part of the process, give it a defined interface rather than a free hand. A typed tool interface (for example MCP) lets an agent create findings or fetch a project while permissions, audit and the data boundary stay in the platform.

Documentation-plus-review hours as a percentage of testing hours.

If the first two fall and the third does not rise, the change is working.

One way to do this in practice is by using PentestPad .

It’s is a pentest reporting and project-management platform designed around this workflow: 20+ imports (Burp Suite, Nessus, Qualys, Nuclei, OpenVAS, CSV, JSON), reusable vulnerability templates, a CVSS calculator, custom branded DOCX/PDF/XLSX reports, a white-label client portal, an AI writing assistant that can run against your own self-hosted LLM, an MCP server for agents, and a choice of EU cloud or full self-hosting.

PentestPad is built to be driven by software as well as by a person at a keyboard, and the model doing the driving can sit inside your own network.

The writing assistant works from what a tester already has. Hand it scanner output, a Burp finding, a screenshot or a log file, attach the evidence, and it returns a structured finding written to the instructions your organization has defined, so the draft arrives in your format rather than a generic one.

PentestPad is the knowledge base, a local model does the reasoning, and a terminal harness is wired to both.

Access to the context of the tested environment greatly helps PentestPad outperform other generic automated vulnerability detection tools.

items.title: The AI Threat Horizon: Why Speed, Edge AI and Baselines Are Our Best Defense
items.summary: Unit 42 examines the evolution of AI-driven cyberattacks and outlines proactive defense strategies for security teams. The post The AI Threat Horizon: Why Speed, Edge AI and Baselines Are Our Best Defense appeared first on Unit 42 .
items.details:
Unit 42 examines the evolution of AI-driven cyberattacks and outlines proactive defense strategies for security teams.

AI-driven attacks are on the rise, transitioning from theoretical risks to real-world threats. Recent investigations reveal that criminals are using AI to accelerate attacks at scale. We have observed attackers leveraging AI agents to execute context-aware commands with real-time decision-making . In one campaign that we observed, a highly persistent threat actor utilizing AI generated 117 unique scripts across multiple languages and executed over 8,000 unique commands in just 12 days whereas normal attackers usually do dozens of commands with a few scripts for similar time periods.

The behavioral difference between human operators and AI agents is staggering. In one attack we observed, humans acted followed by an agentic AI attacker. In the first (human attacker) phase, time between commands averaged roughly 24 seconds. The hackers made typographical errors, repeated manual checks and demonstrated environment confusion. On the other hand, in the agentic phase of the attack, we observed flawless, zero-syntax-error commands with a median gap of just 1.4 seconds.

When an AI agent is instructed to execute aspects of an attack, it rapidly scans networks, attempts to escalate privileges and utilizes legitimate native tools to blend in. Because of AI’s machine-speed execution, our Mean Time To Respond (MTTR) metrics must improve considerably. Attack isolation and near real-time response are now critical mandates. If we wait hours to react, an AI agent can have already enumerated our cloud infrastructure and extracted or encrypted our data.

To effectively defend against AI-powered attacks, defenders must employ AI-powered tools. This should be done right where the attacks happen. Defenders should also strive to understand the behaviors that separate AI-based attacks from normal operations, whether fully autonomous or partially controlled by a human.

To counter adversaries operating at automated speeds, defense must occur where the attack takes place. Leveraging AI on the edge, specifically on endpoints and Next-Generation Firewalls (NGFW), is a major strategic necessity. Edge-based AI can process telemetry instantly, making split-second decisions to terminate malicious web shell sessions or block active privilege escalation attempts locally.

Edge AI is also exceptionally fast. In our own product deployment, edge AI operated in milliseconds rather than taking minutes like agentic LLMs. It can function independently of cloud access or continuous network connectivity. This capabilities shift is crucial for several key reasons:

Even if an attack vector is used to temporarily disable network traffic to operate silently, local edge AI maintains detection coverage

It enables defenders to catch and isolate threats at the earliest possible stage

It safeguards sensitive corporate data locally without requiring telemetry or proprietary data to be transmitted to the cloud for analysis

Despite their speed, agentic AI attackers have a foundational weakness that affects any attacker: They enter your environment without information. To operate, they must perform extensive reconnaissance, port sweeping and environment enumeration. This is where defenders hold the ultimate upper hand through comprehensive AI analytics.

Winning against machine-speed adversaries requires turning the advantage into real-time detection through automated data fusion and detection. By collecting telemetry across diverse network, endpoint, identity and cloud sources, normalization can map these distinct data streams into a single, cohesive schema. Advanced stitching can then merge related events across these disparate sensors into unified, context-rich stories rather than disconnected events.

Observing these integrated stories allows AI analytics engines to establish baselines of normal organizational behavior across the entire ecosystem. While establishing baselines has been longstanding best practice, AI analytics engines have made it easier for defenders to create these and keep them up to date.

Because threat actors lack this context, their automated attempts to rapidly map the terrain inevitably trigger detectors against established baselines, immediately exposing their presence across our detection layers.

Detection alone was never enough to stop machine-speed threats, but the issue is even worse in the era of AI attacks. Detecting an intrusion minutes after it begins still leaves defenders vulnerable if no immediate action is taken, and in those minutes an agentic AI attacker can cause significant damage to your organization. To truly close the loop against these attacks, organizations must combine real-time detection with automated response capabilities, enabling instant attack isolation and automated remediation before critical systems or data can be compromised.

While the sheer volume and speed of AI attacks can seem daunting, there is a positive takeaway: AI-empowered threat actors are not invisible, and their campaigns are entirely detectable. Every attack that we observed triggered alerts, and deep forensic investigations enabled us to reconstruct the attack lifecycles.

The cybersecurity basics still matter. The tools we have relied on as defenders in the past, including XDR solutions, network monitoring and active prevention rules, are still essential and relevant today. We do not need to throw away our playbooks; we simply need to use them differently. By utilizing our existing tools to automate isolation, leaning into AI on the edge for real-time response and trusting our baseline knowledge of our own environments, we are well-equipped to win against the next generation of threats. Crucially, unifying these tools into a cohesive SOC platform connects the dots across the enterprise — where vertical integration and correct platform usage ultimately drive vastly superior security outcomes.

If there’s one thing to take away from this, it is that Mean Time to Detect and Mean Time to Respond (MTTD and MTTR) are still king. But if we want to win these battles, detection and response times must drop to minutes, not hours.

To safeguard your organization against the unprecedented speed and adaptability of AI-driven threats, now is the time to evaluate your defense strategy. Ensure your enterprise is equipped with advanced detection and response capabilities, deploy robust security technologies across your endpoints, network, cloud and identity environments, and continuously refine their configurations to eliminate coverage gaps. Take action today to empower your security operation with the real-time visibility, automated response, and contextual intelligence needed to stay ahead of next-generation adversaries.

items.title: InfraTrust warns of exploited supply chain flaws in network appliances
items.summary: Eclypsium's November InfraTrust report warns that most infrastructure security advisories addressing exploited vulnerabilities over the past month involve flaws in third-party software bundled into products rather than code developed by the vendors themselves. [...]
items.details:
Eclypsium's November InfraTrust report warns that most infrastructure security advisories addressing exploited vulnerabilities over the past month involve flaws in third-party software bundled into products rather than code developed by the vendors themselves.

The November InfraTrust Pulse report tracks 373 new security advisories published by 23 infrastructure vendors between October 15 and November 19, covering 3,880 vulnerabilities.

Of these advisories, 98 were rated critical, and 38 contained vulnerabilities listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

However, 33 of those 38 advisories fixed exploited flaws in bundled software components, primarily PHP, Node.js, and OpenSSH.

These vulnerabilities pose additional risks for enterprises, as even after a software developer releases a security fix, organizations must wait for infrastructure vendors to incorporate it into their products.

"Your exposure to exploited flaws depends on how quickly each vendor rebuilds its products after an upstream fix ships," the report reads.

An example of this is the two PHP vulnerabilities known as PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) highlighted in last month's InfraTrust report , which are now being exploited in attacks against Palo Alto Networks and Check Point firewalls.

In both cases, threat actors chained the PHP vulnerabilities with other flaws to gain root access to compromised devices, with Check Point reporting destructive attacks that deployed data-wiping malware on VMware ESXi hosts .

As of November 20, PHP2Shell fixes were either partially available or had yet to be released for affected products from Fortinet, Juniper, Lenovo, HPE, Netgear, HP, and Siemens.

The November 19 release of another 18 PHP security advisories further complicated patching efforts for infrastructure vendors and their customers.

With administrators dealing with an increasing number of infrastructure vulnerabilities to address, InfraTrust says to prioritize the following flaws for immediate patching this month:

Cisco Expressway: CVE-2026-76466, a critical vulnerability added to CISA's KEV catalog on November 20. On November 23rd, CISA flagged this flaw as actively exploited after Russian cybersecurity firm F6 spotted hackers using it to gain root privileges.

Palo Alto Networks and Check Point: The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and CVE-2026-123039 in Check Point gateways. Check Point warned that this flaw was being actively exploited to gain root privileges and establish persistence on vulnerable devices since late October.

Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator: CVE-2026-114625, a critical vulnerability with a CVSS score of 9.9 that was exploited in zero-day attacks .

Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and FTD: CVE-2026-76418, affecting devices configured for remote-access VPNs. The flaw was exploited in attacks to crash devices .

SonicWall SonicOS: CVE-2026-19868, allowing multifactor authentication bypass on VPNs configured with single sign-on. SonicWall warned that it received reports that the flaw was exploited in zero-day attacks .

Administrators should also prioritize installing Fortinet's October hardening updates, which addressed numerous vulnerabilities discovered using AI models.

As AI makes it easier to discover and exploit vulnerabilities, InfraTrust warns that organizations must take additional steps to protect their devices while waiting for vendors to release security updates.

These include removing management interfaces from the Internet, segmenting them internally to limit lateral movement, and investigating previously exposed devices for backdoors that may remain even after security updates are installed.

"Patching is table stakes, but what you do before the patch is available and after the exploit hits will determine whether you survive," the report concludes.

items.title: Our 2026 Cybersecurity Predictions: What We Got Right, What We Got Wrong, and What Changed
items.summary: Rapid7’s annual Security Predictions webinar returns on December 10, bringing our experts together to explore what the year ahead could hold for cybersecurity. Before sharing our predictions for 2027, we’re grading last year’s calls: that geopolitical tensions would reshape cyber threats, insider threats would dominate breach root causes, and context would become the new currency of cyber performance. Register here for the 2027 Security Predictions webinar . As security leaders work through their priorities for 2027, those predictions offer a useful starting point. The year reinforced several of the concerns we highlighted, while developments in attacker behavior and AI added new dimensions to the discussion. Looking at how those themes unfolded helps us understand what remains relevant and where our thinking needs to evolve. Geopolitics shaped cyber targeting, with businesses caught in the middle Our prediction that geopolitical fault lines would redraw the cyber battlefield earned an A-, as regional conflicts created opportunities for espionage, disruption, and public pressure throughout 2026. Cyber operations allowed adversaries to pursue those objectives below the threshold of open warfare, with commercial organizations exposed alongside government and critical infrastructure targets. Rapid7 Intelligence tracked a spike in retaliatory activity following regional military escalations in late February. State-directed actors pursued espionage and data theft, while hacktivist personas amplified the impact. Rapid7 also assessed that stolen information was likely to be passed from state actors to hacktivist groups for public release, extending the consequences of an intrusion beyond the initial compromise. That chain from state actor to hacktivist release makes an organization’s exposure harder to judge from its own location or industry alone. Customers, suppliers, infrastructure, and perceived political associations can attract attention, bringing a seemingly routine commercial relationship into a much wider conflict. Examining those dependencies during response exercises uncovers difficult decisions early, particularly where protecting a service or containing an incident requires agreement across security, operations, legal, and executive leadership. items.details:
Rapid7’s annual Security Predictions webinar returns on December 10, bringing our experts together to explore what the year ahead could hold for cybersecurity. Before sharing our predictions for 2027, we’re grading last year’s calls: that geopolitical tensions would reshape cyber threats, insider threats would dominate breach root causes, and context would become the new currency of cyber performance.

Register here for the 2027 Security Predictions webinar .

As security leaders work through their priorities for 2027, those predictions offer a useful starting point. The year reinforced several of the concerns we highlighted, while developments in attacker behavior and AI added new dimensions to the discussion. Looking at how those themes unfolded helps us understand what remains relevant and where our thinking needs to evolve.

Our prediction that geopolitical fault lines would redraw the cyber battlefield earned an A-, as regional conflicts created opportunities for espionage, disruption, and public pressure throughout 2026. Cyber operations allowed adversaries to pursue those objectives below the threshold of open warfare, with commercial organizations exposed alongside government and critical infrastructure targets.

Rapid7 Intelligence tracked a spike in retaliatory activity following regional military escalations in late February. State-directed actors pursued espionage and data theft, while hacktivist personas amplified the impact. Rapid7 also assessed that stolen information was likely to be passed from state actors to hacktivist groups for public release, extending the consequences of an intrusion beyond the initial compromise.

That chain from state actor to hacktivist release makes an organization’s exposure harder to judge from its own location or industry alone. Customers, suppliers, infrastructure, and perceived political associations can attract attention, bringing a seemingly routine commercial relationship into a much wider conflict. Examining those dependencies during response exercises uncovers difficult decisions early, particularly where protecting a service or containing an incident requires agreement across security, operations, legal, and executive leadership.

Our prediction that insider threats would dominate breach root causes drew attention to risks ranging from employee negligence to deliberate access selling. During 2026, reporting on ransomware recruitment attempts reinforced concerns about attackers seeking cooperation from people inside organizations, while the growing use of AI agents broadened the conversation about insider risk. As agents gain access to business systems and take actions on an organization’s behalf, questions about permissions, oversight, and unintended consequences increasingly extend beyond human users.

Our blog on insider recruitment in ransomware campaigns explored an approach by Medusa to a BBC journalist, offering payment in exchange for access. It illustrated how attackers combine financial incentives, persuasion, and pressure to pursue legitimate credentials, giving organizations a concrete reason to include recruitment attempts in awareness programs and response planning.

The wider access economy also remained significant, although credentials appearing for sale do not establish that an employee willingly supplied them. External compromise and exposed systems continued to provide routes into businesses, with AI-assisted vulnerability discovery adding further pressure. Our prediction captured an important concern, while the year reinforced the need to distinguish deliberate insider cooperation from other ways attackers obtain and misuse access.

Our prediction that context would become the new currency of cyber performance earned a B, largely because understanding an environment has always been fundamental to protecting it. During a year shaped by AI-driven vulnerability discovery, however, the ability to connect a new finding with exposed systems, attacker activity, and business consequences became particularly valuable when teams had little time to decide how to respond.

Our analysis of the ASOS incident explored that challenge after an unauthorized notification reached customers through the retailer’s own app. With the route of compromise still unclear, the incident raised questions about access to customer communications platforms and how investigators connect activity across accounts, integrations, and third-party services.

The same need for context applies to remediation, where an advisory alone cannot determine whether interrupting a critical service is justified. Teams need to know where affected technology is running, how attackers could reach it, and which mitigations are practical. Bringing asset information, threat intelligence, and operational knowledge together remains essential to making those decisions with confidence.

Across all three themes, the year reinforced how closely security decisions depend on understanding relationships: between organizations, between identities and access, and between technical weaknesses and business consequences. Those connections will remain relevant as AI changes how technology is used and how threats develop.

Join Rapid7’s Security Predictions webinar on December 10 to explore those shifts with our experts and consider what they could mean for your priorities in the year ahead.

Red Hat recommends treating all kernel errata as security-relevant. Given the kernel's fundamental role, any bug has a higher chance of impacting system security, even if that impact only becomes clear after a fix is published. Therefore, Red Hat prioritizes delivering fixes that improve our customers' overall security posture.

Because of this proactive approach, a patch may be associated with a CVE assignment at a future date. Red Hat Product Security has rated this update as having a security impact of Important. A Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) base score, which gives a detailed severity rating, is available for each vulnerability from the CVE link(s) in the References section.

Python is an interpreted, interactive, object-oriented programming language, which includes modules, classes, exceptions, very high level dynamic data types and dynamic typing. Python supports interfaces to many system calls and libraries, as well as to various windowing systems.

items.title: Hackers Exploit Two GeoServer Flaws as Researchers Warn of Unauthenticated RCE Chains
items.summary: Threat actors are actively exploiting two newly patched security flaws in GeoServer, according to watchTowr. The vulnerabilities in question are CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243, details of which are below - CVE-2026-120705 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An arbitrary file read vulnerability that could enable an attacker to access local text files readable by the GeoServer process or fetch
items.details:
Attackers are exploiting two newly patched GeoServer flaws that could enable file disclosure and authorization bypass without authentication.

Threat actors are actively exploiting two newly patched security flaws in GeoServer, according to watchTowr .

The vulnerabilities in question are CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243, details of which are below -

CVE-2026-120705 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An arbitrary file read vulnerability that could enable an attacker to access local text files readable by the GeoServer process or fetch adversary-selected HTTP or HTTPS URLs by means of a single unauthenticated Web Feature Service (WFS) request.

CVE-2026-129243 (CVSS score: 8.8) - An incorrect authorization vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to invoke OWS operations that are otherwise protected by service security rules.

Advisories for both the flaws were published on November 24, 2026, in the following versions -

CVE-2026-120705: org.geoserver:gs-wfs-core - 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7

CVE-2026-120705: org.geotools:gt-metadata - 35.2, 34.6, and 33.7

CVE-2026-129243: org.geoserver:gs-ows - 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7

"Attackers sent error-based exploit probes to validate that the server is vulnerable by creating and invoking stored queries," the preemptive exposure management firm said in an X post today.

Yordan Ganchev, principal threat intelligence specialist at watchTowr, said the vulnerabilities can allow attackers to bypass security restrictions, interact with internal services, retrieve stored secrets, forge authentication credentials, and deserialize and run code on affected systems.

"On November 25, we observed in-the-wild exploitation against our global honeypot network in the early morning hours leveraging CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129244," Ganchev said. "Threat actors from multiple IP addresses were observed validating vulnerable systems on the internet by creating stored queries on GeoServer machines, checking whether they were created, and deleting them immediately afterward."

Eye Security, which discovered and reported CVE-2026-120705, said the flaw can be combined with two other vulnerabilities in the same product to create an unauthenticated remote code execution chain -

CVE-2026-129245 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use of a hard-coded signing key ("geoserver") vulnerability in the "remember me" functionality that could be exploited to forge administrator authentication. (Fixed in org.geoserver:gs-main versions 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7)

CVE-2026-120704 (CVSS score: 7.2) - An improper control of the generation of code vulnerability that could allow an administrator, or anyone with access to an administrator session, to execute arbitrary code as the user running GeoServer. (Fixed in org.geoserver.security:gs-sec-jdbc versions 3.0.2, 2.28.6, and 2.27.7)

In a hypothetical attack chain, a bad actor can follow the steps below -

Exploit CVE-2026-120705 to access "users.xml," a file containing GeoServer usernames and password hashes, and obtain the password representation along with the static signing key extracted from the security configuration ("security/config.xml").

Exploit CVE-2026-129245 to forge a valid administrator authentication cookie by using the predictable signing key and the stored password representation without having to know the administrator password.

Exploit CVE-2026-120704 to abuse an administrator-controlled JDBC configuration to execute code from an uploaded native library on both Linux and Windows versions of GeoServer.

According to the project maintainers, CVE-2026-129245 is also part of a five-step unauthenticated remote command execution chain that involves -

CVE-2026-129244 (CVSS score: 6.9) - WFS stored query exception discloses data directory path

CVE-2026-129243 (CVSS score: 8.8) - Service security rules bypassed with a prefixed service name such as x/WFS

CVE-2026-120705 (CVSS score: 8.6) - Unauthenticated WFS GetFeatureById XML injection

CVE-2026-129245 (CVSS score: 9.2) - Predictable "remember me" key allows administrator session forgery

CVE-2026-129242 (CVSS score: 8.6) - Deserialization in JDBC user and role services allows administrator code execution

"An attacker who obtains an administrator password digest, through any file disclosure or a copy of the data directory, can log in as that administrator," GeoServer maintainers said. "Changing the key in security/config.xml does not help when the same file disclosure also reveals the key."

Jonah Burgess, a Senior Security Researcher at Rapid7, who goes by the online alias CryptoCat has been acknowledged for independently discovering and reporting the five-step unauthenticated remote command execution chain on August 2, 2026.

"Prefixing the Web Feature Service (WFS) name, as in x/WFS, slips past the admin-only rule for stored queries. GeoServer turns escaped text in a saved query into live xi:include elements, which leaks the files holding the remember-me key and the admin password digest," the researcher said .

"Those two values forge an administrator cookie without cracking the password. As admin, the attacker points a JDBC user service at an uploaded HSQLDB database, and the bundled driver deserialises a stored value that runs commands."

In light of active exploitation of two of the flaws, users are advised to update to GeoServer versions 2.27.7 , 2.28.6 , and 3.0.2 released over the past month as soon as possible.

The development comes a little over three months after another critical flaw in GeoServer ( CVE-2026-76904 , CVSS score: 9.8) witnessed active exploitation efforts as a zero-day.

items.details:
U.S. Treasury's FinCEN confirms unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems and takes some systems offline as a precaution.

The U.S. Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network ( FinCEN ) has been hit by a cybersecurity incident that resulted in "unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems," the bureau said on Tuesday. As a precaution, it has taken some systems offline.

The bureau collects suspicious activity reports and other Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) filings from banks and other financial institutions and analyzes them to fight money laundering and terrorist financing.

The BSA E-Filing website is still up, although some services may be temporarily unavailable. The agency has not named the systems it reached or those it took offline.

To support filers affected by the disruption, the bureau is extending some filing deadlines: covered reports originally due between November 18 and December 29 can now be submitted until December 30.

A relief order issued the same day, FIN-2026-R002, applies to three groups:

Financial institutions that used Secure Direct Transfer Mode (SDTM), the channel for sending batches of BSA reports directly from their own servers, as of November 18

Companies required to file a beneficial ownership information report during the covered window

Individuals required to update a FinCEN Identifier during the same window

All other Bank Secrecy Act obligations stay in force, including the duty to monitor for suspicious transactions. The service alert says urgent suspicious activity information can still reach law enforcement through the Financial Institutions Hotline, 1-866-556-3974, which is not affected by the disruption.

The disclosure followed days of filing trouble. Filing providers reported failures in automated batch submissions beginning November 18, and the bureau posted a notice about the disruption to SDTM late last week, according to a filing outages report by the markets news site The Deep Dive.

The bureau has not said whether the intrusion caused those outages. The order grants the relief because of a "service disruption" and does not mention the cybersecurity incident.

Nor has the agency said when the access began, whether any data was viewed or taken, or who was responsible. No group has publicly claimed the intrusion so far. Those answers matter because of what the bureau holds: reports of suspicious financial activity filed by financial institutions nationwide.

The incident is not Treasury's first in recent years: in December 2024, a China-linked group used a compromised BeyondTrust API key in an earlier Treasury breach that reached department systems and documents. No link between the two incidents has been reported.

items.title: CVE-2026-123903: Critical VMware Directory Service Authentication Bypass affects vCenter
items.summary: Overview On November 24, 2026, Broadcom released VMware Security Advisory VMSA-2026-0011 to address several new vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-123903 , a critical authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service component of vCenter. Broadcom assigned it a CVSSv3.1 score of 9.8 Critical . An attacker who can reach an affected vCenter’s VMware Directory Service (vmdir) over the network can gain access without authenticating. Broadcom's supplemental FAQ distinguishes CVE-2026-123903 from an older vulnerability CVE-2026-123890 , which Rapid7 covered previously when CVE-2026-123890 was reported as being exploited in the wild. Both of these vulnerabilities affect the VMware Directory Service in vCenter and can give an attacker access to the vCenter without credentials. CVE-2026-123890 was reachable over RPC while CVE-2026-123903 is reachable over LDAP. As of this writing, there are no known public reports of exploitation of CVE-2026-123903 in the wild. A public proof-of-concept exploit is available and has been validated by Rapid7 to successfully achieve an authentication bypass. Attackers are known to be targeting vulnerabilities in the VMware Directory Service, therefore Rapid7 recommends remediating exposed systems on an urgent basis outside of normal patching cycles. Mitigation guidance Vendor updates are available for CVE-2026-123903. Broadcom lists no workaround , and these vCenter updates are not eligible for Quick Patch. Rapid7 recommends updating affected deployments on an urgent basis, outside normal patch cycles, using the standard update mechanism for the deployment. Broadcom lists the following available fixed versions to remediating CVE-2026-123903. These fixed versions also remediate several other high and medium severity CVEs from the same advisory (CVE-2026-123904, CVE-2026-123905, CVE-2026-123906, CVE-2026-123907, CVE-2026-123908, CVE-2026-123909): VMware Product Affected Version Fixed Version / Patch VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.x 9.1.2 VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation 9.0.x.x 9.0.2.0300 VMware vCenter 8.0 8.0 U3m VMware vCenter 7.0 Contact Broadcom Support (extended-support customers) VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x 5.2.5 VMware Telco Cloud Platform 3.0 , 4.x , 5.0.x , 5.1.x , 5.2 KB463501 VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure 3.0 KB463501 Note that if vCenter 8.0 U3m was previously installed when remediating CVE-2026-123890, it also fixes CVE-2026-123903 and no further vCenter update is needed. For the latest affected-version and remediation guidance, refer to Broadcom's security advisory and supplemental FAQ . Rapid7 customers Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management (InsightVM), and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-123903 on VMware vCenter Server with an unauthenticated vulnerability check expected to be available in the November 25, 2026 content release. Intelligence Hub Customers leveraging Rapid7’s Intelligence Hub can access Suricata detection rules for detection of the public CVE-2026-123903 exploit. Updates November 25, 2026: Initial publication. November 25, 2026: Add Intelligence Hub section.

items.title: CISA Adds 10 Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
items.summary: CISA has added 10 new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2023-25914 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Path Traversal Vulnerability CVE-2023-25915 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Input Validation Vulnerability CVE-2025-41450 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Authentication Vulnerability CVE-2026-103406 Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Juniper Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router OS Command Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-133275 Mitel MiCollab Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Vulnerability CVE-2026-133303 Mitel MiCollab XML Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-133311 Mitel MiCollab Weak Authentication Vulnerability CVE-2026-133323 Mitel MiCollab OS Command Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-133324 Mitel MiCollab Not Failing Securely Vulnerability CVE-2026-133469 Vates Xen Orchestra Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.
