items.details:
GitGuardian finds 64% of valid secrets discovered in 2022 still worked in January 2026, while validity-only triage misses 46% of critical secrets.

More than 64% still valid after four years: GitGuardian’s State of Secrets Sprawl 2026 found that most valid secrets discovered in 2022 still worked in January 2026, because teams stall on what a revoke will break.

Validity-only triage misses 46% of critical secrets: Prioritize by impact instead, weighing what a credential can access and whether it leaked publicly, and update the risk score as new context arrives.

Revoke last, never first: Issue a replacement, store it in the vault, switch every consumer to the vault call, deploy and monitor, then revoke the original and confirm it no longer authenticates.

Every modern enterprise depends on credentials. This is how humans, systems, and now AI connect securely to data, services, and each other. GitGuardian helps secure that credential layer through three connected capabilities: Detect, Remediate, and Prevent. The journey starts with detection, but credential remediation is where many secret security programs bog down. This is the second of three articles we are releasing to explain how we help address detection, remediation, and prevention.

The first article in this series, “ The Credential Layer Is Expanding Faster Than Security Teams Can See It ,” covered detection across every surface where credentials live. Just knowing they exist is not enough. Teams need to take action to remediate those findings. To do that, they need context around every credential they find.

Without the right context, it is impossible to know what risks the secret carries. It is also difficult to understand which systems rely on those secrets and the risk levels that revoking the secret brings. Nobody wants to break production, but we also cannot allow attackers to leverage those secrets.

The resulting decision paralysis leaves many teams struggling to rotate immediately. Sometimes it can take years for the secret to be revoked finally. That is actually all too common, as shown by GitGuardian’s State of Secrets Sprawl 2026 research that found that 64% of valid secrets discovered in 2022 still worked in January 2026, a full 4 years later.

It would be great if there were a one-size-fits-all solution for remediating every leak; in reality, each one is tied to a specific integration. What we can do is streamline the processes needed to get to the end, making it much easier for organizations of any size. And it does take the whole organization to properly deal with leaked secrets.

A team that discovers an exposed credential rarely has all the authority or knowledge needed to fix it without causing further issues. A security engineer can see it’s valid and dangerous, but that security engineer usually cannot immediately tell which services will fail when it is revoked. Breaking production is considered a much higher risk than the possibility of a stolen and abused secret, so they need to go looking for answers, which is a time-consuming process.

The developers who know where and why a key is used and, hopefully, how to rotate it safely are often busy shipping new features and managing existing requests from the business. An alert in their email that shows only a file path and a secret type asks those busy devs to stop their workflow and launch their own investigation. These requests, all too often, sink into the backlog.

At the same time, the larger the organization, the harder it is to find the right person who knows the answer to “what breaks if this key is revoked?” Application security teams monitor code where keys are used, identity and access management (IAM) teams govern identities that were issued keys, and the Platform Engineering team runs the vaults holding the keys. They all have different perspectives and, in most organizations that are early in their secrets security maturity journey , can only tell part of the story.

Endpoint security teams are also watching what happens at the workstation level. They are beginning to track secrets stored there, as software supply chain attacks have increasingly targeted these plaintext credential stores over the last couple of years. A secret leaked here might even be the triggering event for the rotation in case of compromise from an infostealer. The endpoint team is historically not connected to AppSec or Platform teams.

One credential can touch all these teams while each individual, isolated group sees only its own slice of the credential layer. Now, multiply the communication and coordination issue across hundreds or thousands of potential leaks, and the scale of the remediation problem becomes clearer.

The risk of revoking before fully understanding the fallout is fairly high for the business. This is weighed against potential future abuse. Of course, this math changes during an active breach when the clock is ticking and when exfiltration or lateral movement is already occurring. Those emergencies do not get backlogged. Mature organizations understand that addressing leaks before an emergency arises is the better plan overall, but remediation times are still measured in weeks for most teams. How long a remediation process takes really boils down to how fast and accurately responders can gather and communicate information about the issue. Responders need to know a lot of things, starting with whether the credential works, what it can access, and who owns it before they can even ask questions like “where else does it appear?” and “which systems depend on it?”

For example, envision two valid cloud credentials. One grants read-only access to a single storage bucket, and the second one is a root-level key with administrative control over production. While their privileges and dependent workloads determine the appropriate level of urgency, both require the same level of insight and investigation to triage the remediation process and decide whether the response is a rotation next sprint or a revocation this very second.

The ultimate goal is to remove the leaked key rapidly, but in a way that does not interrupt production or break pipeline builds. Rotating secrets safely simply requires resources and a coordination plan. If this process is always piecemeal and manual, then mistakes are more likely to happen.

A security team that causes an outage once will face resistance the next time it asks to rotate anything.

Validity is the first and clearest signal most responders look at. Alone, this is an incomplete signal. GitGuardian research from the State of Secrets report found that validity-only triage misses 46% of critical secrets such as custom API tokens and SSH keys, because those secrets cannot be verified automatically.

While validity still matters, access to sensitive data or core systems raises urgency. If the leak happened publicly on the internet, that raises the urgency even further. Any risk scoring needs to explain which factors drove it. It also needs to be a living risk score, adjusting for new information as new context arrives. Scoring it once upon discovery is akin to trusting an initial CVSS score in a CVE disclosure. It is a helpful guide but needs to be updated based on what is really going on in your organization. The organization and its risk tolerance will decide what happens next. Having as much information centrally available as possible is key to a rapid response, as responders reach the boundaries of what systems they can actually touch.

Remediation requests should let the developer or platform team act immediately, without requiring the team to repeat the investigation that has already taken place.

Any request to replace a key for a production system should include validity and known exposure locations. It should list dependencies too, and where possible show how it connects to business operations. The more the person picking up the request understands about the issue, the sooner they can act. In an ideal world, all remediation requests would be routed to their named owners. In the messy reality of the enterprise, you will likely need to involve the developer who leaked the secret and gather data from commit attribution or source metadata. We need to establish communication because there is a probability that they will need further instructions or guidance.

Requests should not be ‘thrown over the fence’ and then forgotten about. Follow-up and confirmation about remediation progress should be centrally collected and shared so every department knows where the rotation process is at any given moment. This accountability proves resilience efforts when an auditor shows up.

Engineers need to be enabled with a clean way to communicate once they start the work and once their ticket is ready to close. Routing the work through existing ticketing tools keeps it alongside other engineering work, but those tickets also need to integrate with the responder’s security operational tooli

items.details:
Drupal Fail2Install Exploit Details Emerge as Critical RCE Flaw Faces Active Exploitation | Read more hacking news on The Hacker News cybersecurity news website and learn how to protect against cyberattacks and software vulnerabilities.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added a critical flaw impacting Drupal to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities ( KEV ) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the fixes by November 27, 2026.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-132165 aka Fail2Install (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of remote code execution (RCE) impacting Drupal core.

"Drupal Core contains a not failing securely vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to take over an existing site or execute arbitrary code via the Drupal installer," CISA said. "Under specific conditions, the attacker can use install.php to attempt to reinstall Drupal on the site."

As previously reported by The Hacker News, an attacker can use the installer to attempt to reinstall Drupal, resulting in site takeover or remote code execution under certain circumstances.

According to an independent analysis by Searchlight Cyber, it has emerged that ordinary server resource limits can be abused to trick Drupal into mistakenly believing that an existing website was not installed, enter its installation process via "install.php," create an administrator-controlled account, and execute arbitrary PHP code.

While Drupal has checks in place to determine whether the website is already installed before allowing installation to proceed, the research found that it's possible to bypass these checks by exhausting server resources.

As a result, a failed database connection to the configured database and a failed database check for an existing installation are interpreted as evidence that the website has not been installed, thereby opening the door to a scenario where Drupal allows the installation to proceed but only after winning a race condition that allows a second database connectivity check to pass.

"So if the database refuses the early connections and accepts the later one, all within one request, the installer concludes the site is new and shows its setup forms on a live site," StepSecurity said in an explainer. "

"The installer's database form saves the settings it receives to settings.php. Once an attacker submits that form with their own database settings, the live site points at the attacker's database. The attacker then creates the site's administrator account."

To achieve this, the three resource exhaustion techniques have been put to use -

EMFILE , which refers to a limit on how many files a Linux process can open

"We started with EMFILE, then explored database and TCP limits to determine whether availability failures could become security primitives," the cybersecurity company said.

"Applying this methodology to Drupal uncovered a pre-authentication RCE affecting Drupal 8.9, 9, 10, and 11 across four common deployment combinations: Apache with PostgreSQL, Apache with MySQL, PHP-FPM with PostgreSQL, and PHP-FPM with MySQL."

This behavior can be turned into a pathway for code execution by taking advantage of the fact that Drupal's installer supports SQLite database files and allows the database path to be selected during installation. This is possible because the installer does not enforce restrictions on the file name extension.

"By selecting a path ending in .php under the document root, the installer creates an SQLite database with a PHP extension," Searchlight Cyber said. "Once the installation reaches the site configuration form, Drupal stores the submitted website name inside the SQLite database. By using PHP code as the website name, the payload bytes are written into the .php database file."

While direct access to the generated PHP file is blocked by Drupal's stock .htaccess on a stock Apache deployment, a path-handling weakness in the Apache RewriteRule could be exploited to achieve arbitrary PHP execution.

"Starting from three system-wide limits, we showed how errors that appear to affect only availability can become primitives for crossing a security boundary," Searchlight Cyber researchers Kevin Gervot and Adam Kues said.

"In Drupal, temporary database failures can produce a FAIL, FAIL, and then SUCCESS sequence that reopens the installer on an existing website and ultimately leads to pre-authentication RCE through an SQLite database containing PHP code."

The issue has been addressed in the following versions -

The addition of CVE-2026-132165 to the KEV catalog follows a report received by the Drupal Security Team that it "was exploited on live sites as early as 2026-11-19 19:00 UTC."

It's worth noting that CVE-2026-132165 is the third Drupal flaw to come under active exploitation this year following CVE-2026-9082 (CVSS score: 6.5) and CVE-2026-118539 (CVSS score: 6.5).

items.title: Microsoft fixes Microsoft 365 bug blocking access to Office apps
items.summary: Earlier this week, Microsoft resolved a known issue that was preventing some Microsoft 365 customers from accessing Office applications. [...]
items.details:
Earlier this week, Microsoft resolved a known issue that was preventing some Microsoft 365 customers from accessing Office applications.

This follows widespread reports on social media and Microsoft's support website about what affected users described as a persistent white screen or square that can't be dismissed, displayed over Office apps' user interfaces or Microsoft 365 sign-in windows.

"We've installed 3 separate versions of 365 on this device, but no matter how we try to get into a 365 app we get stuck on this white screen. I've launched applications in safe mode as well without any luck," one user said.

The company confirmed in a support document updated Monday that a blank dialog box prevented customers from opening Microsoft 365 Outlook, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OneNote, and Access apps.

"When you open an Office application, a blank dialog window might appear. The dialog box doesn't show any text or buttons," Microsoft said . "If you can't dismiss it, you might be unable to continue using the application."

Microsoft says the issue is now fixed in Microsoft 365 Apps Version 2611 (Build 16.0.20625.20142), released last week .

​However, Microsoft says that customers who can't update because of this bug can also upgrade to the latest version from the command line by going through the following procedure:

Run the following command "%programfiles%\Common Files\Microsoft Shared\ClickToRun\officec2rclient.exe" /update user updatetoversion=16.0.20625.20142 .

This is the last in a series of bugs that have affected Microsoft 365 and Office customers since the start of the year.

For instance, in June, Microsoft fixed another issue that blocked Office for the web users from opening Excel and PowerPoint documents , and another that prevented Windows 365 users from downloading the Office suite.

One month later, it resolved a bug that blocked third-party apps from launching Microsoft Office apps like Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Access and from opening documents on Windows systems.

More recently, in September, Microsoft fixed a known issue causing copy-and-paste and autofill failures for Excel users after installing the September 2026 security updates.

That same month, Microsoft also had to temporarily pause the rollout of the KB5002907 Microsoft 365 update to fix a bug that deactivated (and in some cases completely removed) perpetual Office 2016 and Office 2019 installations for some users.

items.title: The Great Escape: Tradecraft insights from an agentic swarm
items.summary: The OpenAI-linked swarm activity in 2026 is fully traceable through public records. This blog analyzes its tradecraft and compares it to early signals and behaviors from current agentic attack activity seen in the wild.
items.details:
The OpenAI-linked swarm activity in 2026 is fully traceable through public records. This blog analyzes its tradecraft and compares it to early signals and behaviors from current agentic attack activity seen in the wild.

The OpenAI-linked swarm activity in 2026 is fully traceable through public records and offers an unprecedented view into how multi-agent AI systems operate and coordinate at scale.

Distilling and documenting the swarm tradecraft may help defenders understand multi-agent operations and communication, and how agents adapt when a path is blocked.

Some documented behaviors may transfer to more purpose-built cyber attack frameworks like ARTEX, including methods to persistently store results, the burst-and-pause timing patterns of reasoning loops, and the self-labeling conventions that can reveal workload assignments and distribution.

Beginning in June 2026 and extending for several months, a collection of OpenAI models conducting internal training and evaluation tasks broke out of their containerized environments and accessed websites and databases via the public internet in ways the company says it did not authorize .

This activity represents a new kind of cyber event: not a malicious intrusion, but an unintentional series of consequences stemming from an agentic swarm , a group of AI agents exhibiting coordinated behavior toward a shared objective. A swarm implies many agents but doesn’t have a rigid count. The main distinction is behavioral; the collective activity of a swarm becomes complex and unpredictable even when individual agents may be explainable. This swarm provided an initial, public glimpse into the behavior and coordination of autonomous, multi-agent operations.

Due to constraints in their evaluation environment, the OpenAI swarm used public internet services as improvised infrastructure, which made the activity visible and traceable. The behaviors exposed revealed methods for persistent probing, iterative payload development, work partitioning and coordination across agents, and adaptation to execution constraints, in ways that are likely to be relevant for understanding agent behavior beyond this just case.

Agentic cyber attack frameworks are now appearing in intrusion activity , with the ability to support scaling to multi-agent operations . These attacker swarms largely replace the use of public internet resources with purpose-built infrastructure that removes some of the artifacts visible. However, documenting our understanding of operational swarm techniques can give defenders a baseline for recognizing behaviors as they move into new environments and contexts. In some cases, we can already see the evidence where these techniques do transfer.

In this post, we’ll explore and document the tradecraft of the escaped OpenAI swarm and conclude by comparing it to early signals and behaviors from the current agentic attack activity seen in the wild.

Swarms are an important concept to track because they can divide work across parallel agents, potentially completing complex tasks faster, though the gains depend on the task and the quality of coordination. Parallel agent coordination was crucial to OpenAI’s ability to solve the Navier-Stokes Millenium Prize Problem, which arrived at a winning solution with a group on the order of 10,000 concurrent agents over the course of 88 hours.

Early evidence suggests swarms transfer effectively to cyber attack problems. The main factors for swarm efficiency are how parallelizable the tasking is, and if the attackers want to pay the inflated token cost. A rough example is using four agents on the same problem, to get it done twice as fast; as Noam Brown of OpenAI said on a Dwarkesh podcast , “Because there are four agents working for half as long, you’re paying 2x more to get an answer twice as quickly.”

AI models undergoing training and evaluation operate inside sandboxed computing environments. These are controlled workspaces where they can write and run code, search for information, and iterate toward solutions. These environments are designed to be both enabling and constraining. They give models room to practice, while limiting what they can reach and do, so that mistakes or misaligned behavior stay contained.

While the techniques employed by the OpenAI swarm may have crossed the thresholds of intended use, they should not be viewed as malicious intent. A useful framing for understanding these techniques is creativity under constraint. The agents were optimized to meet their objectives, and they displayed considerable persistence and ingenuity to that end.

The constraints the agents were working around were layered and understanding them helps explain the motivation behind every technique. The most fundamental was the absence of a browser runtime: Agents operating in text and code environments cannot natively load JavaScript-heavy pages, call browser APIs, or interact with dynamic web content. The creative solution was submitting URLs to a public scanner like “urlquery.net” which provided a real Chromium instance on demand.

This workaround by itself, however, was still not enough. Browsers apply a security rule called the same-origin policy: JavaScript running on one website generally cannot read data from another. Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) lets a destination website explicitly permit access. The agents used public CORS proxies to relay requests when target websites did not grant permission.

They also lacked infrastructure of their own to host payloads or receive data, so they relied on public services such as httpbin, httpbun, and "webhook.site" services capable of testing HTTP requests and responses but not designed for this activity.

In some evaluation environments another constraint applied: Agents appear to have been restricted to GET requests only, with no ability to make outbound POST calls. That is likely what pushed them toward using public wikis as shared state stores , as wiki page edits are a write operation achievable through ordinary browser navigation.

In response to their constraints and in persistent pursuit of their objectives, the swarm developed and refined its tradecraft over time. This included chaining legitimate web services like URL shorteners, CORS proxies (services that relay requests to bypass browser security restrictions), Base64 decode endpoints (services that decode encoded data back into executable web pages), and markdown renderers into extraction pipelines that never required dedicated attacker infrastructure.

Talos observed structured work partitioning across parallel agent instances, iterative probe development, and sandbox identification techniques. The agents coordinated using a variety of identifying tags (e.g., uqscan=claude... , CHATGPTTEST1 , OAI_META_1312 , archive_test=20261004 ). These self-labels, intended as internal tracking strings, became the primary cross-campaign fingerprint linking multiple disparate operations.

To better understand the flow, we will detail the activity of the swarm in a seven-step chain, aligning the purpose of the action with the publicly accessible internet services used.

A separate orchestration layer, Coordinate (COORD), runs above the chain rather than within it. When multiple agents execute the same chain in parallel, COORD governs how work is divided between them — for example, URL shorteners (“da.gd”, “is.gd”) distribute identical payloads to multiple instances; structured identifiers ( ?uniq0–19 , node= , validation=v<unix>_<county>_<req> ) partition tasks and track completion. The COORD layer distinguishes a swarm from a single agent running sequentially.

The swarm's operational techniques evolved over time. Early activity relied on silent CDX enumeration, querying public web archive indexes to map target sites and using a single exit node. By the peak operational phase, the swarm was running against multiple simultaneous targets with structured work partitioning, sandbox identification, and covert exfiltration beacons. To better understand these events, we can reconstruct from public records the unauthorized access to Australian government websites .

The agent silently maps the target site structure by querying Common Crawl's CDX, a searchable database of every URL the archive has ever crawled. This allows enumeration of all potentially relevant target URLs, without the server ever being contacted.

The request in Figure 2 returns archived URL paths, MIME types, timestamps, and status codes. The agent discovers objective-relevant Tableau visualization endpoints at “vizprod.aihw.gov.au” without ever touching AIHW servers.

Effect: Agent identifies the target: vizprod.aihw.gov.au/t/Public/views/AGE-115/...

The agent writes a self-contained HTML page with embedded JavaScript. This payload uses the Tableau JS API to load a dashboard; enumerate its parameters, worksheets, and filters; then beacon the extracted data out via an image request.

items.title: Securing Grandma's groceries with Pierre Cadieux
items.summary: Pierre takes us back to his early days on help desks in the 90s, where learning to correlate logs between Windows and Unix systems sparked the curiosity that eventually led him to security.
items.details:
Pierre takes us back to his early days on help desks in the 90s, where learning to correlate logs between Windows and Unix systems sparked the curiosity that eventually led him to security.

This month, Amy is joined by Pierre Cadieux, Research Lead for Intelligence Efficacy at Talos. Pierre takes us back to his early days on help desks in the 90s, where learning to correlate logs between Windows and Unix systems sparked the curiosity that eventually led him to security. It’s a great look at how someone who has seen the industry evolve over decades stays grounded and keeps their edge. We also get into what’s kept Pierre at Cisco for nearly ten years. He talks about why he prioritizes the human impact of our work, the importance of knowing when to step away from the keyboard, and how his background in anthropology actually informs the way he approaches threat intelligence today.

Amy Ciminnisi: I've known you since you were in Talos IR, which was not too long ago. But tell me a little bit about your professional journey, because I know that definitely was not the start of it.

Pierre Cadieux: I worked at an ISP as part of the help desk back in the mid-90s. I was one of the people who people would call up and say, "Hey, I've got this computer I just bought, how do I get it on the internet?" I did a lot of learning about what TCP/IP was, what networking was, how to connect things via various different types of connections — whether it be an actual hard-coded network connection or a dial-up connection — and was able to get some expertise around guiding people through that process.

Then I moved to a technology company in San Diego and worked on their help desk. One day, someone called me up and said, "You know how to read Linux logs, right? Or Unix logs, UCS logs, Linux logs." I said, "Yeah." They said, "You know how to use Windows — you're a Windows Server guy, too." I said, "Yeah." They said, "I need you to sit in this chair, look at these two screens — one is a Windows box, one is a Unix box. I need you to be a correlation engine."

So, I looked at the timestamps for both of them, and helped to figure out what was happening because we were having an emergency, an incident, and they had nobody that could look at both. People at that point in time in this organization were very much, "I am doing just Unix things and only know Unix things. I am Windows things only. I only know one of those things." They didn't cross the streams. I could talk both. So I sat in the chair, I stared at both screens and I helped them to track the timeline of what was happening, which ended up being an intrusion exploiting a vulnerable SSH server that was compromised. That changed my course into security.

I spent a number of years in internal security for a number of organizations and got into leadership positions, even CISO positions, leading security teams globally for financial services, for instance, and others. Then I moved into consulting and did that for a number of years as well.

PC: I'm hitting my ten-year anniversary at Cisco in January. What keeps me at Cisco and Talos is the flexibility of my work. I'm able to, within most bounds, choose what I work on and how I get things done. I have a lot of flexibility in my workday, day-to-day. I work West Coast hours compared to most of my team members who are East Coast. So I sometimes work early shifts with them and am done by the early afternoon. Or sometimes I have to work with folks who are over in Asia Pacific, and I'm working later.

What does it mean to be "blue collar" for the blue team? Ryan Fetterman discusses the realities of detection engineering, and shares his philosophy on building a career in security without burning out.

Amy looks back at the incredible journeys that brought past guests to the world of threat intelligence.

Ever wonder how someone goes from studying human viruses to leading cybersecurity teams? In this Humans of Talos, we’re joined by Martin Lee, EMEA Lead, to talk about his journey into the industry.

items.details:
A former OpenAI employee accused of bugging company offices was granted $1 million bond after investigators found hundreds of audio files.

A former OpenAI employee accused of concealing a covert recording device at the company's San Francisco offices will be allowed to be released from jail on a $1 million bond, a San Francisco federal court judge ruled Tuesday.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, was arrested on October 9, 2026, for allegedly bugging the artificial intelligence (AI) company's offices with the aim of recording sensitive conversations.

Subsequent court filings have pointed out that Alfozan was in touch on WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi royal family, as well as expressed interest in moving back to Saudi Arabia following OpenAI's initial public offering (IPO).

He has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of 5 years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by 3 years of supervised release.

"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the ChatGPT-maker said at the time.

Alfozan pleaded not guilty to the charges during his appearance in San Francisco federal court earlier this month.

According to CNBC , the decision comes after prosecutors told the court last week that they had "found no new evidence to support the theory that Mr. Alfozan was stealing trade secrets, or to support the speculation that he was acting as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia."

However, they said investigators have found hundreds of audio files on the defendant's personal devices, including dozens of recordings of meetings or conversations that took place at OpenAI throughout September 2026.

Some of these involved meetings with OpenAI customers and contained material protected by attorney-client privilege, prosecutors said, adding he possessed a photograph of what's believed to be a term sheet for a "strategic partnership" between OpenAI and another company.

"What the defendant did or intended to do with those audio files remains under investigation," they said.

Under the bail conditions, Alfozan will be required to wear a GPS ankle monitor, observe a curfew from 7 p.m. to 7 a.m., stay within the Northern District of California, and avoid airports and train and bus stations. He is expected to be released on Wednesday morning.

"There is no spy story that we're talking about right now," U.S. Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse said, per The Wall Street Journal . "The government doesn't have that."

items.title: Hackers now exploit critical Drupal RCE flaw to hijack sites
items.summary: The Drupal security team has confirmed that a critical vulnerability that lets attackers hijack unpatched sites has been actively exploited since at least Thursday. [...]
items.details:
The Drupal security team has confirmed that a critical vulnerability that lets attackers hijack unpatched sites has been actively exploited since at least Thursday.

Drupal is a content management system (CMS) commonly used by large organizations, including government entities, major research universities, and high-profile enterprise and media organizations.

The security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-132165, was discovered by Anthropic's OSS Scanner and can be exploited by anonymous users to gain remote code execution or take over vulnerable sites by abusing the Drupal installer.

"Drupal core ships with an install.php file for installing Drupal core. Under specific conditions, an attacker can use the installer to attempt to reinstall Drupal. This can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution," the Drupal security team warned last Wednesday. "Some exploit paths are mitigated if the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php."

While it wasn't initially flagged as abused in the wild, in an update to the original security advisory, Drupal warned that this flaw has been "exploited on live sites as early as 2026-11-19 19:00 UTC."

Websites using the paid Drupal Steward Web Application Firewall (WAF) service are already protected from known attack vectors, but admins are still advised to upgrade to the latest available Drupal version in case other attack vectors are discovered.

Those who can't immediately upgrade should block access to /core/install.php in the web server configuration or the .htaccess file in the web root to secure the Drupal installer.

On Tuesday, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has also added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog and ordered federal agencies to secure their systems against ongoing attacks by Friday, November 27.

"These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise," the agency warned. "While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities."

Since November 2021, CISA has tagged five Drupal vulnerabilities as abused in the wild, two of which have also been exploited by ransomware groups.

items.details:
An update for cifs-utils is now available for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.2 Extended Update Support.

Red Hat Product Security has rated this update as having a security impact of Important. A Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) base score, which gives a detailed severity rating, is available for each vulnerability from the CVE link(s) in the References section.

The SMB/CIFS protocol is a standard file sharing protocol widely deployed on Microsoft Windows machines. The cifs-utils packages contain tools for mounting shares on Linux using the SMB/CIFS protocol. The tools in this package work in conjunction with support in the kernel to allow one to mount a SMB/CIFS share onto a client and use it as if it were a standard Linux file system.

items.title: Hackers Exploited CVSS 10.0 Hex.pm RCE Flaw to Compromise 6 Package Registry Servers
items.summary: An attacker ran operating system commands on Monday on six production servers of Hex.pm, the package registry that Elixir and Erlang developers fetch their dependencies from. The flaw used in the attack had been in the registry's code since February 2016, and the team that maintains the service had every server on a patched build within about 15 minutes of the first malicious request. Checks
items.details:
Attackers exploited a decade-old Hex.pm flaw to execute commands on six servers, with potential exposure of account data and private packages.

An attacker ran operating system commands on Monday on six production servers of Hex.pm , the package registry that Elixir and Erlang developers fetch their dependencies from.

The flaw used in the attack had been in the registry's code since February 2016, and the team that maintains the service had every server on a patched build within about 15 minutes of the first malicious request.

Checks since then found no sign that any package was changed. Whether the attacker read account data such as email addresses, password hashes, and two-factor authentication secrets could not be ruled out, the team said.

Everyone with a hex.pm account has been logged out because the maintainers replaced the keys that sign sessions and access tokens. They advise account holders to take these steps:

Reset two-factor authentication by setting up a new authenticator entry, and store the new recovery codes.

Log back in to the client with mix hex.user auth or, for Erlang projects, rebar3 hex user auth.

Update the Hex client when the next release ships, expected within days, with a new registry signing system.

Watch for phishing. Exposed email addresses may be misused, so check that links in any email about Hex go to hex.pm.

API keys do not need to be replaced, according to the team: they are random 128-bit values stored only as HMAC-SHA256 hashes, which it says cannot realistically be brute-forced. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt, which slows guessing but does not stop it for weak passwords, so changing them still matters.

Developers who never created a hex.pm account and only fetch public packages have nothing to reset, Peter Ullrich, one of the report's authors, said in a maintainer clarification on the Elixir Forum. Those who signed up with GitHub should still log back in to their clients, and reset two-factor authentication if they enabled it.

Until the new client ships, the advice is to fetch packages only from repo.hex.pm and to avoid third-party mirrors. The registry signing key has not yet been replaced, and it was among the credentials the attacker could have read.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-129514 with the maximum CVSS score of 10.0, sat in the parser hex.pm used to read request bodies sent in an Erlang data format. That parser ran before routing and authentication, so an unauthenticated POST request to any address on the site could reach it.

The decoding function was meant to be safe, and it did block dangerous terms such as functions, but it accepted maps with a __struct__ key, which allowed a request body to pose as any Elixir struct the application had loaded.

The safety check that would have stopped this was removed from the code on February 23, 2016, which is where the flaw's age comes from. Exploitation before Monday has not been established.

A crafted struct ran nothing by itself. It caused an error, and the error reporting code then inspected the struct. That inspection, via the Ecto and DBConnection database libraries, led to a point where the server called a function of the attacker's choice, which then ran operating system commands with the permissions of the registry's service account.

The security advisory lists hex.pm as affected from February 23, 2016 until Monday. The fix commit makes the decoder reject any term containing a map with a __struct__ key, and every hex.pm server was running it by 18:31 UTC on Monday.

Load balancer logs recorded 69 exploit requests between 18:16 and 18:29 UTC on Monday, all from two addresses, the Hex.pm team said in its incident report yesterday. Files created by the exploit appeared on six web servers, in one case just 3 milliseconds after the request. Three of those servers joined mid-attack, when a restart brought up machines still on the vulnerable build.

To check the packages, the team compared every database table against a copy taken two minutes before the first exploit request and traced each difference to normal activity. The 23 releases published during the attack all match the audit log, no older release was changed, and the package and registry files written that evening match the database records.

Database reads, shell commands, environment variables and direct reads from file storage were not logged. For that reason, "we cannot rule out that the attacker accessed data stored in the database," the team wrote. That database holds email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, two-factor authentication secrets and session data, and private packages could also have been read without leaving a trace.

The checks found no leftover shells and no new accounts or cloud keys in the audit logs. Who was behind the attack is unknown. Activity from the two addresses going back to late last week suggests the attacker built a local copy of hex.pm to test against, according to the team.

A separate security report describing the same flaw arrived by email at 19:07 UTC on Monday, after the attack had ended. By yesterday morning the team had replaced every credential the attacker could have read except the registry signing key. On Monday night it reported the breach to the Swedish data protection authority, to CISA in the United States and to ENISA in the European Union.

Alongside the incident, maintainers of three widely used Elixir libraries disclosed flaws of their own involving structs built from untrusted data, and shipped fixed versions yesterday. These are separate disclosures, not further attacks on Hex.pm.

Each needs its own conditions to be exploited. The Ash flaw requires keyset pagination with a client-supplied cursor, certain sort field types, and a signing secret left at its unset default, according to the Ash advisory .

The db_connection flaw "is not exploitable in db_connection alone," the DBConnection advisory says, because another component must first decode untrusted data into structs. The Flop flaw has similar conditions around its pagination cursors, according to the Flop advisory .

The exploited flaw sits in the hexpm server code, not in the Hex client, so organizations that run their own copy of the registry are affected until they deploy the patch.

Important: gdm security, bug fix, and enhancement update

An update for gdm is now available for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.

Red Hat Product Security has rated this update as having a security impact of Important. A Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) base score, which gives a detailed severity rating, is available for each vulnerability from the CVE link(s) in the References section.

The GNOME Display Manager (GDM) provides the graphical login screen. The screen is shown shortly after boot, after log out, and when switching the current user.

gdm: Missing authorization on CreateRemoteDisplay allows autologin as arbitrary users, including root (CVE-2026-132858)

Make smartcard method default when smartcad is inserted in login screen (gdm) (JIRA:RHEL-287797)

Unable to switch users with smartcards with virtual terminals disabled (RHEL-10) (JIRA:RHEL-307213)

For more details about the security issue(s), including the impact, a CVSS score, acknowledgments, and other related information, refer to the CVE page(s) listed in the References section.

items.title: Microsoft confirms authentication issues after November updates
items.summary: Microsoft has confirmed that customers may experience authentication issues after installing November security updates that address a high-severity remote code execution vulnerability. [...]
items.details:
Microsoft has confirmed that customers may experience authentication issues after installing November security updates that address a high-severity remote code execution vulnerability.

Tracked as CVE-2026-118737 , this security flaw was found in the Windows Remote Procedure Call Runtime and stems from a timing-dependent authentication weakness that unauthenticated attackers can exploit to remotely execute code without user interaction on unpatched systems.

Microsoft says the November security updates represent the first phase of NTLM message-signing improvements, which reduce exposure to relay attacks by ensuring authenticated NTLM sessions always establish a cryptographic session key and negotiate real message signing.

However, as Microsoft explained in an updated support document, the new security improvements introduced to address this vulnerability may also cause authentication failures on patched devices.

"Microsoft is aware of compatibility issues affecting some third-party apps and devices, including authentication proxy servers, single sign-on (SSO) solutions, and application packaging solutions that use NTLM authentication," it said.

"This issue can occur when such a proxy device does not correctly implement the NTLM protocol. For example, an affected device might set the NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_TARGET_INFO flag in its CHALLENGE_MESSAGE but provide an empty or incomplete TargetInfo field."

While a fix is not yet available, Microsoft said affected apps and devices return an NTLMSSP_CHALLENGE message with an empty "Target Info List" in network trace signatures or Target Machine fields with "Not Found" values in event logs.

As a temporary workaround, the company advised customers to go through the following procedure on affected systems:

Set the ClientAllowUnsignedNtlm REG_DWORD registry value under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0 to 1 (the value used for clients that do not offer SIGN)

Check whether the affected device or application supports a configuration that uses Kerberos authentication or whether the vendor provides a software or firmware update compatible with the NTLM signing requirements introduced by CVE-2026-118737 .

If neither option is available, contact the device or software vendor to request an update that complies with the NTLM protocol requirements described in 3.1.5.1.2 Client Receives a CHALLENGE_MESSAGE from the Server .

However, Microsoft said the ClientAllowUnsignedNtlm registry setting is a short-term solution and may be removed in the future.

"Updating the affected product or using a compatible authentication configuration is the recommended long-term resolution," it noted.

Since it addressed installation issues affecting the November 2026 cumulative updates, Microsoft has also confirmed that this month's security updates are causing Windows activation failures and SQL Server performance issues .

The company is also investigating a known issue that may break printing documents with complex formatting for customers who have installed the latest Windows updates.

CrowdStrike has been named a Leader in the inaugural 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) Systems. We have also been named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for SIEM. We believe this placement reflects one core principle: The unified CrowdStrike Falcon® platform provides the foundation where expert SOC agents gain a complete view of the enterprise, reason over key decisions, and act at machine speed.

Security teams are drowning in detections. Analysts spend hours piecing together context across dozens of point tools, while every new data source increases SIEM costs. Now AI agents operate across the enterprise with elevated privileges, adding a new attack surface the SOC has to defend. We believe the inaugural Gartner Magic Quadrant for ISOC Systems reflects a long-expected shift: SIEM can no longer stand alone as a system of record.

We believe Gartner created this new market to evaluate security operations as one integrated system rather than a collection of separate tools integrated with SIEM.

We feel this shift points to a new operating model: the agentic SOC, where expert agents investigate and respond to every detection and analysts direct the work. Read on to discover the five essential requirements for the agentic SOC and learn why we believe only CrowdStrike delivers them natively on a unified platform.

The agentic SOC starts with SIEM, and SIEM starts with data. Agents are only as good as the context they act on. When data is fragmented across silos, agents reason on incomplete information and inherit the same blind spots that have long plagued human analysts. CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM brings first-party and third-party signals together so every agent works from the same complete picture.

Native Falcon platform telemetry across endpoint, cloud, identity, exposure management, and AI agents comes in with no added ingest cost. Certified data pipelines, built on CrowdStrike Falcon® Onum and validated by CrowdStrike Falcon® Complete , bring in detection-ready third-party data and filter out noise at ingestion. Customers can reduce data storage costs by up to 50%, 2 and federated search reaches data wherever it lives.

The same data layer also addresses agent activity. CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian shows what an AI agent did and interacted with on the endpoint, including prompts, tool calls, MCP servers, skills, and subagents. This data is correlated with identity and endpoint data, so a compromised agent surfaces already connected to its owner and host.

The agentic SOC needs adversary context to understand how disparate alerts may relate to the same attack. Unified data provides visibility across the environment, while adversary intelligence helps explain how threat actors operate and who may be behind an attack.

Intelligence from CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations , which tracks more than 290 named adversaries , is built into the Falcon platform and applied natively to detections in Falcon Next-Gen SIEM. Agents correlate related alerts into unified investigations, using adversary intelligence to recognize known tradecraft, understand potential threats, and help prioritize them based on business risk.

AI is changing how employees work. From browser-based AI applications and coding assistants to autonomous agents that access tools, data, and systems, AI is becoming an integral part of everyday workflows. Much of this activity happens on the endpoint, where AI interactions can translate into real system actions.

Securing employees’ use of AI requires more than visibility into which applications employees use or what they send to AI models. Security teams must also understand what agents are instructed to do, how they communicate, and what they execute. No single feature can do this alone. It’s only possible with multiple security capabilities working in concert across each organization’s AI estate.

CrowdStrike® Falcon Guardian™ brings together complementary security mechanisms to deliver visibility, protection, and response across AI interactions and agent activity. Here, we detail these capabilities and how they help security teams better understand AI activity and risk.

AI activity spans multiple layers, from employee interactions with AI applications to agents communicating with models and executing actions on the endpoint. Securing this activity requires complementary visibility and security controls at each layer.

Securing a single layer is not sufficient to gain a full picture of all AI usage. A browser extension, for example, would only be able to look at traffic going to and from web-based agents and AI tools, completely missing activity agents executed on the endpoint. Similarly, agent hooks would miss AI web apps and any prompts transiting through there; it would not be able to discover agents on the endpoint. The CrowdStrike Falcon® sensor is capable of seeing AI traffic, supplies runtime visibility, and allows for agent discovery of even dormant agents; however, it does not directly hook into the agent’s inference framework. It takes multiple layers to get the full picture and to have sufficient security and visibility to apply defense in depth.

Falcon Guardian extends security beyond individual AI interactions to the communications and underlying system activity that AI agents generate.

Visibility is only the starting point. Falcon Guardian enables security teams to enforce policies across supported AI interactions and agent activity, with controls tailored to where AI operates.

For supported browser-based AI interactions, policies can report, block, or transform content to help govern AI use and protect sensitive information. Agent-level hooks extend policy enforcement into supported AI agents, enabling security teams to inspect interactions and block potentially dangerous actions before execution.

At the operating system level, the Falcon sensor provides independent runtime protection, detecting and blocking supported malicious behavior even when an agent's initial action was permitted.

items.details:
Unknown attackers have reportedly breached an open-source intelligence analysis system at the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)

​Unknown attackers have reportedly breached an open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysis system at the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), according to a source familiar with the matter.

The source told The New York Times , which first reported the incident, that the cyberattack was carried out using the ARTEX AI-powered penetration testing framework and also affected the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency.

While the CIA and the ODNI have not yet replied to a request for more details regarding this incident, no classified data or systems were exposed in the breach.

"The hack did not involve our classified networks or classified information, and no other systems are currently at risk," the source said.

Hours after the CIA security breach was reported, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) also disclosed that it's investigating a cybersecurity incident involving unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems. After detecting the attack, the agency took some systems offline as a precaution and told banks to use the Financial Institutions Hotline to file reports, since some services may be unavailable.

"Treasury is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and third-party forensic examiners to determine the scope and impact of the incident," a FinCEN official told BleepingComputer. "In the meantime, as a proactive measure, we have taken certain FinCEN systems offline and provided exceptive relief for filers that are not able to submit reports as a result of the disruption."

BleepingComputer has also learned that, while forensic analysis remains ongoing, there is no evidence of any breach of beneficial ownership databases or the Bank Secrecy Act.

FinCEN is the Treasury Department's financial crimes unit and the country's official Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU), protecting the nation's financial system from illicit activities by sharing financial intelligence with domestic and international law enforcement agencies.

One week ago, the US National Security Agency's classified network also suffered a days-long outage , but the agency blamed scheduled routine maintenance and said its mission-critical capabilities remained fully operational.

These incidents follow a series of other cyberattacks that have led to security breaches at other US federal agencies in recent years.

For instance, two years ago, the Silk Typhoon Chinese state-backed hacking group hacked the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) , another Treasury Department office that administers economic and trade sanctions programs.

The same threat group also breached the Treasury's Office of Financial Research , and it reportedly infiltrated the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (a Treasury Department office that reviews foreign investments for national security risks).

More recently, as BleepingComputer reported over the weekend, hackers reportedly breached the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC) . However, it is unclear how the attackers gained access, when the breach occurred, or whether they stole any information from the compromised systems.

This follows a claim by the ShinyHunters extortion group that it breached the FBI's recruitment website, FBIJobs.gov, prompting an FBI investigation that led to the arrests of multiple suspected ShinyHunters members , including a Canadian cybersecurity executive reportedly linked to the attack.

items.details:
GreyNoise links a campaign affecting 22 organizations and targeting Check Point Management servers to suspected AI-driven offensive tooling.

An unknown threat actor has been using artificial intelligence (AI)-driven offensive tooling in a campaign targeting Check Point Security Management servers, impacting 22 distinct organizations across the world.

The intrusion activity, tracked by GreyNoise under the moniker GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13), is assessed to have targeted organizations in the financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing sectors across the U.K., Ireland, France, Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia, and the U.S.

Confirmed attack activity has been recorded between October 17 and November 2, 2026, with the threat actor using 99 IP addresses to conduct scanning, exploitation, and control. Most of these IP addresses are associated with disposable network infrastructure.

The campaign has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. It's suspected that the attackers are relying on agentic harnesses and systems for vulnerability scanning, exploitation, and automatic interaction with compromised assets.

The threat actor has also been observed using tools like Nmap, Chisel, Impacket, Paramiko, and other Python scripts to carry out internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement on victim environments.

"We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created," GreyNoise said.

In one case, the attackers have been found using an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500 , a critical flaw in Rejetto HFS, in early October 2026 to obtain control of the server and issue commands, including adding an SSH key to the "/root/.ssh/authorized_keys" file.

Subsequently, GT13 is said to have used the compromised server as a relay for follow-on operations centered around saving command results and exfiltrating data from 24 previously compromised Check Point Security Management servers. The attackers also unsuccessfully attempted to deploy a Linux implant named ZULT to the compromised Rejetto HFS server.

"The GT13 adversary had access to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers before they compromised the HFS server," the cybersecurity company said. "We could not determine when or how the attacker gained access to those Check Point assets."

The attackers also moved to burrow deeper into one of the victim networks, using a script for a now-patched Check Point flaw ( CVE-2026-16232 ) to launch over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point Management Servers to -

Steal firewall databases and internal certificate authority files

Unload security policies, effectively disabling firewall protections

Conduct internal network reconnaissance and attempt lateral movement

The post-compromise activity also involved attempts to target other enterprise systems, such as Citrix NetScaler ( CVE-2023-4966 ), Ivanti Connect Secure ( CVE-2024-21893 ), VMware vCenter ( CVE-2021-21972 and CVE-2023-34048 ), Microsoft Exchange ( CVE-2021-26855 and CVE-2021-34473 ), and Microsoft Netlogon ( CVE-2020-1472 ).

In tandem, the threat actor has attempted to exploit various other security flaws, including, but not limited to -

GreyNoise has theorized that GT13 has in its possession a "mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus" that it uses to weaponize vulnerabilities, scan for susceptible assets, and exploit them to gain access to systems that can be later used as operational relays or true targets.

"The activity reported by the GreyNoise article involves CVE-2026-16232, a previously disclosed vulnerability with patches already available, and does not represent a new vulnerability or exploitation technique," Sergey Shykevich, Director, Threat Intelligence at Check Point Software Technologies, told The Hacker News.

"Our priority remains ensuring customers apply the available updates and follow Check Point’s published hardening guidance to restrict management access and identify suspicious activity."

An unknown threat actor has been using artificial intelligence (AI)-driven offensive tooling in a campaign targeting Check Point Security Management servers, impacting 22 distinct organizations across the world. The intrusion activity, tracked by GreyNoise under the moniker GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13), is assessed to have targeted organizations in the financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing sectors across the U.K., Ireland, France, Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia, and the U.S. Confirmed attack activity has been recorded between October 17 and November 2, 2026, with the threat actor using 99 IP addresses to conduct scanning, exploitation, and control.

items.title: Com-Affiliated Hackers Hijack Cloud Accounts via Vishing for Data Theft and Extortion
items.summary: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 has disclosed that it's tracking and has responded to "numerous waves of vishing attacks" orchestrated by Com-affiliated threat actors since August 2026 that have led to data theft and extortion attempts. The attacks have targeted financial services, healthcare, and legal services located in the U.S., the U.K., and Australia. Other targets include construction,
items.details:
Com-affiliated hackers use vishing, session hijacking, and unauthorized MFA enrollment to steal corporate cloud data and extort victims.

Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 has disclosed that it's tracking and has responded to "numerous waves of vishing attacks" orchestrated by Com-affiliated threat actors since August 2026 that have led to data theft and extortion attempts.

The attacks have targeted financial services, healthcare, and legal services located in the U.S., the U.K., and Australia. Other targets include construction, high-technology, transportation, manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, insurance, and real estate sectors.

"The victims share a common profile: they hold large volumes of high-impact corporate data where exposure carries severe regulatory, legal, or market consequences," Unit 42 said . "These attackers targeted financial services organizations about twice as often as healthcare organizations in August 2026, but healthcare overtook financial services in September."

The activity has been attributed to a number of threat clusters , including -

CL-CRI-1116 (aka Redact, formerly BlackFile), first observed in January 2026

CL-CRI-1192 (aka Helix and UNC6671), first observed in June 2026

CL-CRI-1264 (aka Vortex), first observed in September 2026

CL-CRI-1274 (aka Cinder), first observed in September 2026

Intrusions typically commence with voice phishing, with the attackers posing as IT staff to resolve a purported authentication issue and direct the victim to a phishing page personalized to their organization.

Once the AiTM kit captures credentials and session tokens, the attackers quickly enroll their own multi-factor authentication (MFA) devices, abuse cloud utilities and, in a few instances, deploy malicious browser extensions to exfiltrate data and extort victims.

The harvested authentication data is used to authenticate to victim environments, typically by routing such requests through residential proxy networks and commercial VPNs. The adversaries then seek to establish multi-layered persistence by registering their MFA devices, generating cloud infrastructure temporary credentials, authorizing unapproved third-party OAuth applications; enumerate sensitive data; evade defenses by modifying mailbox rules and clearing security alert events; and harvest data from cloud platforms.

"Attackers associated with CL-CRI-1264 establish initial access through vishing, where they pose as internal IT support and direct employees to servers using subdomains tailored to each targeted organization," Unit 42 said.

"These servers act as adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) proxies that pass user credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) approvals to the attackers in real time. Attackers have targeted employees on both their corporate workstations and personal mobile devices."

CL-CRI-1264 has also been observed enrolling unauthorized MFA devices within minutes of authenticating to establish persistence, often reusing a single device named Pixel 10a across compromised accounts. The attack chains involve automated data exfiltration using Python scripts to harvest information from Microsoft 365 mailbox, OneDrive, and SharePoint.

Once data is exfiltrated, the threat actor sends Microsoft Teams messages directly to employees at victim organizations, claiming data theft and instructing them to visit a TOR-hosted ransom negotiation site.

The second new cluster to emerge around the same time is CL-CRI-1274, which has also leaned on vishing for initial access and leveraged the Microsoft Graph software development kit (SDK) to collect and exfiltrate data from the victim's SharePoint and OneDrive environments.

"Afterwards, the attackers used a compromised account to send extortion messages internally via email and Microsoft Teams, ultimately directing recipients to a Tor-hosted negotiation site," Unit 42 said.

The cybersecurity company said it also observed the CL-CRI-1192 attackers using a malicious browser extension named "Google Chrome" that's said to have been sideloaded onto the browser after enabling Developer Mode. The add-on performs a number of malicious actions, such as -

Stealing local/session storage and authentication cookies for Microsoft and Google accounts

Scanning pages for QR codes to capture login/MFA tokens

Implementing a command-and-control (C2) remote control module via Chrome DevTools Protocol to capture screenshots, dispatch input events, steal clipboard contents, and allow remote site navigation.

"We assess with moderate confidence that the attackers associated with CL-CRI-1192 developed this malicious browser extension as an alternative method to extract credentials from desktop and laptop devices running Chromium-based browsers such as Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge," Unit 42 said.

"The extension might also be shared with and used by other Com-affiliated attackers, although we currently have no evidence to suggest this."

One of the defining traits of the threat actors is their use of "apex" domains that impersonate single sign-on (SSO) portals, IT support pages, and passkey configuration services for each of the targeted organizations.

Also shared among the attackers is an AitM phishing kit called Doko's Panel that allows them to steal authenticated sessions and then abuse them to access connected software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms like SharePoint, Salesforce, DocuSign, and Slack to exfiltrate data of interest.

"The same persona behind Doko's Panel has been observed actively recruiting 'experienced callers' via Telegram, specifying requirements including fluent English with no accent, and advertising six-to-seven-figure weekly returns — evidence of the professionalized vishing-as-a-service model that complements the phishing kit ecosystem," Push Security noted in a report published earlier this May.

Microsoft has also revealed cloud-based intrusions in which threat actors have employed passkey and SSO lures to obtain unauthorized access and add their own authentication methods to set up persistence, as well as conduct high-volume Microsoft Graph activity, SharePoint and OneDrive downloads, and mailbox collection through REST APIs.

"Rather than employing custom tools, the threat actors primarily leveraged native cloud utilities and selectively limited executions and persistence deployments," Unit 42 said. "Cybercriminals like Bling Libra and other Com-affiliated threat actors are pivoting away from encryption, enabling them to move at greater speed across their intrusion lifecycle while still achieving their objectives."

items.title: WordPress Blocks Six Backdoored WP Connect Plugins Before Malicious Releases Go Live
items.summary: WordPress has removed six WordPress plugins developed by WP Connect after they were backdoored on November 22, 2026, to enable arbitrary code execution on sites that have them installed, following a suspected compromise of the developer's account. The WordPress plugins team has proactively detected and blocked the threat before it could be officially released. Visiting each plugin listing now
items.details:
WordPress blocked malicious releases of six WP Connect plugins containing backdoors designed to enable arbitrary code execution.

WordPress has removed six WordPress plugins developed by WP Connect after they were backdoored on November 22, 2026, to enable arbitrary code execution on sites that have them installed, following a suspected compromise of the developer's account.

The WordPress plugins team has proactively detected and blocked the threat before it could be officially released. Visiting each plugin listing now serves the message: "This plugin has been closed as of November 22, 2026, and is not available for download. This closure is permanent."

The names of the affected plugins and the malicious versions are listed below -

These plugins have been collectively installed on more than 3,600 WordPress sites, according to WordPress security company Wordfence. The supply chain compromise is being tracked as CVE-2026-135202 (CVSS score: 9.8). It remains unpatched.

"Each release silently loaded the same remote-control module, which phones home to an attacker-controlled server, executes any PHP code it is sent, and exposes a full command set for running shell commands, stealing password hashes, and planting webshells," security researcher Chloe Chamberland said .

Specifically, the plugins come with a backdoor module ("includes/airwp-online.php") that runs on every request, sends site information (site URL, PHP, WordPress, and OS versions, and the server user) to a hard-coded command-and-control server ("tascredit-pay[.]com"), and runs PHP code returned by the server via eval().

Dump the users table including login, email address, and password hashes

Drop a web shell into the uploads directory or to a path of the attacker's choosing

Register an hourly WP-Cron hook that runs attacker-supplied code

As a result, an unauthenticated attacker in control of the site can execute arbitrary code on the server and take complete control, facilitating credential theft and persistence through web shells and cron hooks that outlast the plugin removal.

Because the malicious versions were never released and blocked due to WordPress's new cooldown protections as part of its Protect The Shire initiative, sites running these plugins are unlikely to be affected. However, it's essential that site owners check their websites to make sure that they are not running one of the compromised versions and remove them as soon as possible.

"Unlike a typical vulnerability, this was not a coding mistake, and there is no patch: the malicious code was added deliberately and committed to each plugin's WordPress.org repository," Chamberland said. "Taken together, this strongly suggests that the developer's WordPress.org account was compromised and used to push the malicious releases, rather than that the vendor shipped this code intentionally."

The disclosure comes as URLscan.io revealed that an unspecified WordPress site had been infected by multiple cybercriminal campaigns, with attackers attempting to disable or remove scripts belonging to competing threat actors.

The site carried "thirteen separate ClickFix injections from three distinct kits [LOM, ErrTraffic, and Macfinger], alongside seven further malicious loaders," it said . "Several of the injections attempt to remove each other's code and overlays, and one injection disables another through a JavaScript naming collision. Five of the thirteen injections resolve their next-stage infrastructure from Polygon smart contracts, a technique known as EtherHiding ."
