items.title: NGINX HTTP/2 Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-123633
items.summary: Technical analysis of CVE-2026-123633, an NGINX HTTP/2 use-after-free flaw, with details on affected versions, sanitizer tests, and patch guidance. The post NGINX HTTP/2 Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-123633 appeared first on Unit 42 .
items.details:
Technical analysis of CVE-2026-123633, an NGINX HTTP/2 use-after-free flaw, with details on affected versions, sanitizer tests, and patch guidance.

CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free vulnerability in NGINX HTTP/2 that may let an unauthenticated attacker cause a denial of service. In the CVE record, F5 says code execution may be possible when address space layout randomization (ASLR) is disabled or bypassed.

CVE-2026-123633 affects NGINX servers that accept HTTP/2 client connections and proxy requests to a backend when free worker connections run low. A fragmented request can leave an active connection marked reusable. Under connection pressure, NGINX can close that connection and free memory the active request still uses.

F5's CVE record scores the issue 9.2 Critical under CVSS 4.0. The NGINX security advisories page labels the issue medium and lists versions 1.19.7 through 1.30.6 and 1.31.0 through 1.31.8 as affected. F5 credits memN0ps (Palo Alto Networks Unit 42) among the reporters.

NGINX 1.30.7 on the stable branch and 1.31.9 on the mainline branch contain the fix. F5 also lists affected NGINX Plus releases .

Administrators should review HTTP/2 reverse-proxy exposure and upgrade to a fixed NGINX release or a vendor package containing the CVE-2026-123633 fix.

Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed above through the following products and services:

Organizations can access tailored adversary intelligence, direct analyst consultations, and specialized exposure tracking through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services and its Deep and Dark Web Service .

If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the Unit 42 Incident Response team .

While researching NGINX, I independently found the HTTP/2 connection-state defect now tracked as CVE-2026-123633.

An unauthenticated client can send a fragmented HTTP/2 request that leaves an active connection marked as reusable. When the server resolves a hostname during the request and free connection slots run low, NGINX can reclaim that connection mid-request and free memory its DNS resolver is still using.

I reproduced the use-after-free with AddressSanitizer (ASan) on builds of unmodified NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 source. The NGINX security advisories page lists 1.19.7 through 1.30.6 and 1.31.0 through 1.31.8 as affected and 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 as fixed releases.

I reported the HTTP/2 use-after-free privately to F5. F5's CVE record scores it 9.2 Critical under CVSS 4.0 and 8.1 High under CVSS 3.1. The NGINX security advisories page labels it Medium.

In my ASan test on a Debian guest, ASan stopped NGINX at the first read from freed DNS lookup memory.

The resolver path in my test stems from the HTTP/2 connection bug tracked as CVE-2026-123633. CVE-2026-123634 is a separate DNS resolver vulnerability fixed in the same release.

I also found a memory disclosure vulnerability that leaked a libc pointer. I used the address to calculate the libc base and work around ASLR when chaining the disclosure with CVE-2026-123633. I reported this additional bug to F5 as a separate issue. From an attacker VM, I achieved pre-authentication remote code execution on a target VM as the non-root NGINX worker. The chain required a non-default NGINX configuration, and some attempts did not open a shell.

F5 assessed the memory disclosure as a behavior limited to a non-typical configuration and has not assigned it a CVE at the time of writing, so I am leaving out its details and the exploit steps.

NGINX marks a connection reusable when it can close that connection under pressure. Stream creation should clear the reusable mark once a request starts, but ngx_http_v2_create_stream() leaves it set in affected releases.

When a client sends only part of an HTTP/2 HEADERS frame header, ngx_http_v2_handle_connection() marks the connection reusable and returns early. The code below shows that decision:

The reusable mark lets NGINX reclaim connections stalled on partial frames before they exhaust the worker's slots.

The client then sends the remaining header bytes. ngx_http_v2_create_stream() builds a live stream and increments the active stream counter, but returns with the reusable mark still set:

NGINX now has a live request on a connection that its cleanup logic still considers reusable.

The 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 fixes clear the reusable mark at stream creation with ngx_reusable_connection(h2c->connection, 0) . Figure 1 shows the sequence in affected releases:

The stale reusable mark lets NGINX reclaim a live connection when it needs a free slot. In my test, a request-time DNS lookup opened a new socket and triggered the drain.

My test used an HTTP/2 proxy route with a variable upstream. The variable evaluated to a hostname that was neither a literal IP address nor a configured upstream group, so NGINX looked it up during the request. The lookup also had to open a new resolver UDP socket.

The worker opens a new UDP socket only if it has none for the selected nameserver. Cached answers and in-flight lookups also skip the socket-allocation drain I tested.

Opening the DNS socket needs a connection slot, so ngx_get_connection() runs a drain check first. ngx_drain_connections() acts once free slots fall to one sixteenth of worker_connections or below while at least one reusable connection exists. The drain function then selects entries from the tail of the reusable queue, sets each connection's close flag, and calls its read handler:

My test client closed its socket with zero linger after completing the frame, leaving NGINX with an active request on a reset connection. When connection pressure triggered the drain, the HTTP/2 read handler tried to send GOAWAY on that socket.

A successful write would have left the request running, but the write failed with Connection reset by peer , so NGINX finalized the connection and request. The ASan free stack passes through ngx_http_upstream_check_broken_connection() .

Request cleanup reaches ngx_resolve_name_done() , which frees the resolver state while the original lookup still holds a pointer to it.

items.title: Rackspace shuts down Spot cloud platform after security breach
items.summary: Rackspace is shutting down its Rackspace Spot cloud platform after a security breach allowed hackers to access customer Kubernetes clusters and secrets, giving customers until December 8 to migrate their services and download their data. [...]
items.details:
Rackspace is shutting down its Rackspace Spot cloud platform after a security breach allowed hackers to access customer Kubernetes clusters and secrets, giving customers until December 8 to migrate their services and download their data.

Rackspace Spot is a cloud platform that allows organizations to deploy and manage containerized applications using Kubernetes.

The company announced the shutdown in a new security notification sent to customers and obtained by BleepingComputer, saying it had decided to discontinue the service after reviewing the incident.

"Following a review of the situation, Rackspace has made the decision to wind down the Rackspace Spot service. This decision is being made to provide a clear path forward for customers," reads the notification.

Rackspace says the service will be permanently discontinued on December 8, 2026, at 5 PM Central Time, when all remaining workloads will be terminated, and customer data will no longer be accessible.

Customers have been instructed to retrieve their data and migrate their workloads to different platforms before the deadline.

The decision comes after hackers breached Rackspace Spot on November 17 using compromised credentials, allowing them to create unauthorized pods in customer Kubernetes clusters, read Kubernetes Secrets, and list nodes and volumes.

Rackspace discovered the intrusion on November 18 following a customer report and disabled access to the platform's administration console while securing its infrastructure. Service was restored on November 21 following an extended outage.

"An unauthorized party gained access to parts of the Spot platform and may have read cluster Secrets and files on storage volumes," Rackspace said.

The company says the affected Spot environment is segmented from its core infrastructure and that it has not identified evidence of unauthorized access to its core systems or the environments of other Rackspace customers.

Rackspace is now instructing all Spot customers to treat their API tokens, refresh tokens, kubeconfigs, and Kubernetes Secrets as potentially compromised, regardless of whether they previously received a breach notification.

Customers have also been advised to review access logs dating back to November 16 and search for suspicious Kubernetes objects associated with the attack, including:

Suspicious Kubernetes pod and object prefixes: i1 , glm- , and probe

The shutdown announcement has prompted disappointment among Rackspace Spot customers, with some urging the company to reconsider and offering to pay more to keep the platform operational.

In a Reddit discussion , one customer said they believed users would be willing to pay higher prices to keep the service running.

Other customers expressed similar concerns in a separate discussion , with some asking about affordable alternatives and others describing the impact the shutdown would have on their existing infrastructure.

Others praised the service for its affordability, saying alternative cloud providers would be more expensive.

Rackspace has not indicated whether it will reconsider the shutdown decision or offer customers additional time to migrate their workloads.

items.title: Vulnerabilities in Node.js and Brotli Affecting Cisco Products: October 2026
items.summary:
On October 21, 2026, Node.js announced the availability of fixes for multiple vulnerabilities across the following supported release lines: 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x. These vulnerabilities impact critical operations such as the Brotli decoder, DNS resolution, and TLS certificate validation. The vulnerabilities pose risks for remote code execution and traffic interception. For more information, see Node.js Security Release . The following vulnerabilities have a Security Impact Rating (SIR) of High and are addressed in this advisory: CVE-2026-111497 - Brotli decoder out-of-bounds write; potential remote code execution CVE-2026-105482 - DNS resolution truncation involving embedded NUL characters CVE-2026-105483 - TLS hostname validation bypass using fullwidth IP digits CVE-2026-106069 - TLS hostname validation bypass with noncanonical IP addresses For information about Splunk products and offerings, including AppDynamics, see Vulnerabilities in Node.js (CVE-2026-111497, CVE-2026-105482, CVE-2026-105483, CVE-2026-106069) on Splunk Products - October 2026 This investigation was expanded to cover Brotli outside of Node.js on October 30, 2026. The Brotli decoder flaw (CVE-2026-111497), which is in the Google Brotli C decoder, is often bundled with or linked to other software, so products beyond Node.js may be affected. For software that may be affected, see Broccoli2Shell . Important: If a product is not listed within this advisory, Cisco's review indicates that the product is not affected by these vulnerabilities. This advisory is available at the following link: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-oct2026-node-js-Jj3SQ19u
Security Impact Rating: High
CVE: CVE-2026-105482,CVE-2026-105483,CVE-2026-106069,CVE-2026-111497

The SMB/CIFS protocol is a standard file sharing protocol widely deployed on Microsoft Windows machines. The cifs-utils packages contain tools for mounting shares on Linux using the SMB/CIFS protocol. items.title: New Inception extortion gang launches large-scale vishing campaign
items.summary: A newly formed data extortion group named 'Inception' has been linked to a large-scale campaign that targets single sign-on (SSO) credentials of multiple global brands and firms. [...]
items.details:
A newly formed data extortion group named 'Inception' has been linked to a large-scale campaign that targets single sign-on (SSO) credentials of multiple global brands and firms.

A newly formed data extortion group named ‘Inception’ has been linked to a large-scale campaign that targets single sign-on (SSO) credentials of multiple global brands and firms.

The gang surfaced on November 17, claiming seven victims on its extortion site, including chip maker AMD, PepsiCo, Cigna Healthcare, AutoZone, and Lucid Motors, but none of them have publicly confirmed a data breach.

However, cybersecurity company ReversingLabs has been tracking Inception gang's activity and says that it has been operating since late October.

The security firm has confirmed the existence of 21 domains used for SSO phishing, 41 domains believed to be used in campaign infrastructure, and 4 other domains with suspected use.

The researchers identified an extensive phishing infrastructure impersonating dozens of major corporations, including Dropbox, Duolingo, Western Union, Indeed, Activision Blizzard, Riot Games, Twitch, Reddit, Nestlé, Anthropic, Nintendo, Starbucks, McDonald's, Paramount, and NBCUniversal.

The existence of these domains is not proof that those firms have been breached, or even targeted yet, and none have recently disclosed cyberattacks or other related incidents.

The campaign appears to rely on phone-based social engineering rather than email phishing, strongly resembling the tactics used by the infamous ShinyHunters extortion group.

Inception is using legal-themed websites that imitate corporate authentication services, primarily Okta but also NetIQ/OpenText Access Manager.

One of those authentication providers, Okta, published a report yesterday linking Inception to O-UNC-053, a threat cluster it previously associated with ShinyHunters, which has been active since March.

According to Okta, after law enforcement disrupted the ShinyHunters extortion group following the arrest of suspected members [ 1 , 2 ], and the shutdown of the leak site, O-UNC-053 continued to register new phishing domains.

In late October, the activity cluster launched its legal-themed campaign, and in mid-November, the Inception leak site went live, announcing victims that matched previous targeting.

“This gap in publishing on any leak site followed by publishing on a new data leak site with a new brand is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors,” describes Okta .

“Before and after the change in DLS publication, O-UNC-053 maintained consistent infrastructure and TTPs, leading us to assess that the cluster has very likely changed their brand affiliation.”

Inception was quick to respond and dispute the alleged links to other threat actors in an announcement on their extortion page.

The threat actors claimed to operate independently and with no affiliation to any previous group, arguing that overlapping targets and the use of common domain registration and CDN services did not establish operational links.

They also acknowledged that private tooling is circulating among independent threat actors, and using it does not prove affiliation.

To defend against the latest Inception campaign, ReversingLabs recommends enforcing phishing-resistant authentication, including FIDO2 security keys and passkeys, and strengthening help desk identity verification procedures.

DNS, proxy, and identity provider logs dating back to October 21, 2026, should be carefully reviewed for signs of suspicious activity.

items.title: CVE-2026-135614 - Sensitive data redaction bypass in the troubleshooting tool in Amazon ECS MCP Server
items.summary: Bulletin ID: 2026-200-AWS Publication Date: 11/24/2026 11:00 AM PST Description: Amazon ECS MCP Server is an open-source Model Context Protocol server that lets AI agents and assistants manage and troubleshoot Amazon ECS workloads using the operator's AWS credentials. We identified CVE-2026-135614, an issue in the troubleshooting tool of the Amazon ECS MCP Server (awslabs.ecs-mcp-server) before 0.1.36. With the sensitive data setting at its default, the troubleshooting tool returned container environment variable values and secret references from ECS task definitions without the redaction the setting is intended to apply. This might allow a remote actor who can influence the agent's input, for example through prompt injection, to obtain those values. Impacted versions: < 0.1.36 Refer to the article for the most up-to-date and complete information.
items.details:
Bulletin ID: 2026-200-AWS Scope: AWS Content Type: Important (requires attention) Publication Date: 11/24/2026 11:00 AM PST

Amazon ECS MCP Server is an open-source Model Context Protocol server that lets AI agents and assistants manage and troubleshoot Amazon ECS workloads using the operator's AWS credentials.

We identified CVE-2026-135614 , an issue in the troubleshooting tool of the Amazon ECS MCP Server (awslabs.ecs-mcp-server) before 0.1.36. With the sensitive data setting at its default, the troubleshooting tool returned container environment variable values and secret references from ECS task definitions without the redaction the setting is intended to apply. This might allow a remote actor who can influence the agent's input, for example through prompt injection, to obtain those values.

This issue has been addressed in awslabs.ecs-mcp-server version 0.1.36 . We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes. Users should also rotate any credentials stored as plaintext task definition environment variables.

We would like to thank Liu-tong for collaborating on this issue through the coordinated vulnerability disclosure process.

Please email aws-security@amazon.com with any s ecurity questions or concerns.

items.summary: Bulletin ID: 2026-201-AWS Publication Date: 11/24/2026 11:15 AM PST Description: Amazon OpenSearch Service is a managed service for deploying, operating, and scaling OpenSearch clusters in the AWS Cloud. We identified CVE-2026-135414, an issue in snapshot repository registration in Amazon OpenSearch Service. A user with snapshot management permissions on a domain could set a repository endpoint that caused the domain's service-operated nodes to send requests to network destinations that the user specified. This issue is addressed in service software R20260720. We recommend that customers update their domains to R20260720 or later. Impacted versions: Amazon OpenSearch Service service software before R20260720 Refer to the article for the most up-to-date and complete information.
items.details:
Bulletin ID: 2026-201-AWS Scope: AWS Content Type: Important (requires attention) Publication Date: 11/24/2026 11:15 AM PST

Amazon OpenSearch Service is a managed service for deploying, operating, and scaling OpenSearch clusters in the AWS Cloud.

We identified CVE-2026-135414 , an issue in snapshot repository registration in Amazon OpenSearch Service. A user with snapshot management permissions on a domain could set a repository endpoint that caused the domain's service-operated nodes to send requests to network destinations that the user specified. This issue is addressed in service software R20260720. We recommend that customers update their domains to R20260720 or later.

Amazon OpenSearch Service service software before R20260720

This issue has been addressed in Amazon OpenSearch Service service software R20260720. We recommend that customers update their domains to service software R20260720 or later. For instructions, see Service software updates in Amazon OpenSearch Service .

items.title: Turnitin discloses cyberattack affecting customer-facing systems
items.summary: Turnitin disclosed via a statement from its CEO, Chris Caren, that it recently detected unauthorized activity involving certain customer-facing systems. [...]
items.details:
Turnitin disclosed via a statement from its CEO, Chris Caren, that it recently detected unauthorized activity involving certain customer-facing systems.

Educational technology company Turnitin disclosed that it detected unauthorized activity involving certain customer-facing systems and deployed its incident response plan.

In a public statement, CEO Chris Caren says that the incident is being investigated with help from external cybersecurity specialists, and law enforcement and cyber regulators have been notified.

Turnitin is a major education technology firm with a global presence, best known for its AI-generated writing detection, digital grading, academic research integrity checks, and examination proctoring.

According to its website, its software is used in over 16,000 institutions across 185 countries and serves 71 million students.

“We are writing to let you know that we recently identified unauthorized activity involving certain customer-facing Turnitin systems,” reads the letter from the CEO on the platform's website.

“Upon identifying the matter, we implemented our incident response plan, initiated an investigation with external cybersecurity specialists, and notified law enforcement and cyber regulators.”

Turnitin says its systems are fully operational and safe to use, noting that the affected systems do not collect government identification credentials or institutional financial information.

The company said its investigation into the incident remains ongoing and has not disclosed any details about the nature and scope of the unauthorized activity.

If you have any information regarding this incident or other undisclosed attacks, you can contact us confidentially via Signal at 646-961-3731 or at tips@bleepingcomputer.com.

Turnitin continues to monitor its systems for further unauthorized activity, indicating that it is still early to guarantee that the threat has been eliminated completely.

The company has not disclosed whether any user data was accessed or stolen, when the incident occurred, and how many individuals might have been impacted.

Regarding Turnitin service availability, the platform’s status page shows no incidents for November 2026, and the uptime history logs no disruptions.

As of writing, no ransomware groups have publicly taken responsibility for the attack at Turnitin.

BleepingComputer has contacted the firm with questions about the incident, but a company representative said they have no additional details to share at this time.

items.title: CVE-2026-134066 - Query injection via schema-derived identifiers in Graph Explorer
items.summary: Bulletin ID: 2026-199-AWS Publication Date: 11/24/2026 10:30 AM PST Description: Graph Explorer is an open-source tool for browsing and searching graph data, which customers self-host against Amazon Neptune or other graph databases. We identified CVE-2026-134066, an issue in the query construction of Graph Explorer before version 3.2.1. Graph Explorer inserted property keys and labels read from the connected graph database into Gremlin, openCypher and SPARQL query text without escaping. A user with write access to the connected graph database could create a crafted property key or label that, when another user performs a search, causes Graph Explorer to run unintended query logic that accesses and modifies data in that database with Graph Explorer's privileges. On Amazon Neptune, the SPARQL path is not affected. Impacted versions: < 3.2.1 Refer to the article for the most up-to-date and complete information.
items.details:
Bulletin ID: 2026-199-AWS Scope: AWS Content Type: Important (requires attention) Publication Date: 11/24/2026 10:30 AM PST

Graph Explorer is an open-source tool for browsing and searching graph data, which customers self-host against Amazon Neptune or other graph databases.

We identified CVE-2026-134066 , an issue in the query construction of Graph Explorer before version 3.2.1. Graph Explorer inserted property keys and labels read from the connected graph database into Gremlin, openCypher and SPARQL query text without escaping. A user with write access to the connected graph database could create a crafted property key or label that, when another user performs a search, causes Graph Explorer to run unintended query logic that accesses and modifies data in that database with Graph Explorer's privileges. On Amazon Neptune, the SPARQL path is not affected.

This issue has been addressed in Graph Explorer version 3.2.1 . We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

If you cannot upgrade immediately, restrict write access to the graph database that Graph Explorer connects to so that only trusted principals can create or modify property keys and labels.

We would like to thank George Chen for collaborating on this issue through the coordinated vulnerability disclosure process.

Please email aws-security@amazon.com with any s ecurity questions or concerns.

items.title: CVE-2026-134068 - Stack-based buffer overflow in replication origin name parsing in AWS pgactive
items.summary: Bulletin ID: 2026-198-AWS Publication Date: 11/24/2026 10:00 AM PST Description: pgactive is an open source PostgreSQL extension from AWS that provides active-active replication between PostgreSQL databases. We identified CVE-2026-134068, an issue in the replication origin name parsing component of pgactive. Under certain circumstances, an authenticated database user with specific privileges might be able to execute arbitrary operating system commands as the database operating system user. Impacted versions: >= 2.1.0 AND < 2.1.10 Refer to the article for the most up-to-date and complete information.
items.details:
Bulletin ID: 2026-198-AWS Scope: AWS Content Type: Important (requires attention) Publication Date: 11/24/2026 10:00 AM PST

pgactive is an open source PostgreSQL extension from AWS that provides active-active replication between PostgreSQL databases.

We identified CVE-2026-134068 , an issue in the replication origin name parsing component of pgactive. Under certain circumstances, an authenticated database user with specific privileges might be able to execute arbitrary operating system commands as the database operating system user.

This issue has been addressed in pgactive version 2.1.10 . We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Until upgrading, ensure pgactive.pgactive_conflict_handlers is empty on every node and prevent new inserts. Also use only pgactive generated replication slot/origin names and never malformed, manually renamed, or overlong names. On pgactive 2.1.0, also revoke EXECUTE on pgactive.pgactive_parse_replident_name from PUBLIC.

Please email aws-security@amazon.com with any s ecurity questions or concerns.

items.title: Radware discloses breach exposing customer cloud access keys
items.summary: Cybersecurity company Radware says attackers gained access to some of its customers' account details and cloud access keys through an unsecured internal Cloud WAF (Web Application Firewall) management API that was left exposed online. [...]
items.details:
Cybersecurity company Radware says attackers gained access to some of its customers' account details and cloud access keys through an unsecured internal Cloud WAF (Web Application Firewall) management API that was left exposed online.

Founded in 1996 and headquartered in Tel Aviv, Radware now provides application delivery and DDoS protection services to more than 12,500 enterprise and telecom carrier customers worldwide.

In a root cause analysis report shared by an anonymous source with BleepingComputer, Radware says it blocked the originating IP address and access to the internal management API. The company also revoked and replaced all internal account credentials after detecting the breach on Thursday, ten hours after the initial unauthorized API access.

"On 19 November 2026, an unauthorized party accessed an internal-only Cloud WAF management API that was reachable from the Public Internet without requiring authentication," Radware said.

"The confirmed information potentially accessed includes customer contact details, and for a subset of customers, the credentials configured for log export into their self-managed storage (AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, or SFTP)."

The company added that the breach did not expose WAF traffic inspection, certificates, end-users’ data, customer application traffic, or cloud DDoS services and data.

It also "strongly" advised affected AppSec (WAF, BOT) customers to rotate Cloud WAF log export credentials (including Azure Blob Storage keys or SAS tokens, AWS S3 access keys, or SFTP credentials) as soon as possible and review access logs on their cloud storage accounts for unexpected access since at least November 19.

The company is still investigating the breach and whether any API keys or other customer information exposed in the incident were used without authorization, and said it has already received reports from customers about AWS alerts for an unfamiliar IP address attempting to access their log-export buckets.

"WAF traffic inspection and protection have continued without interruption, and we have not identified an impact on the availability or protection of customer applications and services," Radware added. "We have found no evidence to date of changes to customer security policies or of access to customer application traffic."

Radware has yet to issue a public statement regarding the incident or file a breach report with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

BleepingComputer also reached out to a Radware spokesperson with questions about the incident, but a response was not immediately available.

items.details:
Iran-aligned Volant Manticore targets Cyprus and Saudi Arabia using the IPFS-based KuboShell backdoor and a reworked MuddyWater framework.

A previously undocumented Iran-aligned cyber espionage group called Volant Manticore has targeted telecommunications companies, airlines, and critical infrastructure in Cyprus.

Central to the group's operations is a backdoor called KuboShell that uses the InterPlanetary File System ( IPFS ) for command-and-control (C2) and deploys Homa, a post-compromise framework that's a reimplementation of MuddyWater's MuddyC2Go . Evidence indicates that the threat actor has been operational since late August 2025.

Also delivered alongside these tools are Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) programs like MeshCentral and NetLock RMM. In tandem, the group has been observed orchestrating credential harvesting campaigns to collect email and corporate credentials of some of the impersonated organizations.

The use of legitimate RMM tools for persistent access has been a hallmark of the MuddyWater group , although the adversary has since also increasingly deployed its own malware in attacks. Both MuddyWater and Volant Manticore are assessed to be affiliated with Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS).

"While we identified multiple links to MuddyWater, we assess that Volant Manticore likely consists of former MuddyWater operators who branched off from the group and currently operate as a separate threat cluster," Check Point said in an analysis published today. "Volant Manticore's targeting priorities appear responsive to regional geopolitical developments."

This assessment is based on the use of an older MuddyWater framework and its playbook, while diverging from established modus operandi over time to incorporate its own attack methods like credential-harvesting campaigns. The targeting of Cyprus, a country that does not align with MuddyWater's targeting patterns, and the use of separate infrastructure points to a group that pursues its own strategic objectives.

Attack chains have been found to leverage artificial intelligence (AI)-generated personas in bogus CVs to trick targets into clicking on a link to download the complete resume, resulting in the deployment of KuboShell on the victim's system. The activity is said to have been aimed at a Cyprus-based airline that operates flights between Cyprus and Israel.

This includes a shift toward Saudi Arabian healthcare entities, coinciding with escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis.

"This fits the MOIS's track record of targeting hospitals and healthcare providers through cyber operations during military conflicts, in some cases attempting to disrupt their operations," the cybersecurity company said.

As recently as September 2026, the group has been found to launch a phishing campaign against Saudi targets, distributing the backdoor and N-able RMM through two different healthcare-themed ZIP archives named "AI_Healthcare_Seminar.zip" and "Ai_Healthcare_Seminar_Online.zip," respectively. Some of the emails have been sent from a compromised account belonging to a private hospital in Saudi Arabia.

A Windows backdoor, KuboShell uses IPFS for C2 and relies on Pinata to facilitate file transfer over the peer-to-peer (P2P) file-sharing network.

"On startup, KuboShell checks whether it has administrator privileges. If not, it tries to relaunch itself with higher privileges, which triggers a User Account Control (UAC) prompt," Check Point explained.

"KuboShell retrieves the MAC address of the machine's first network adapter and uses it as a unique identifier for each victim. It then registers the host by uploading a file containing hi, saved to C:\Users\Public\<MAC>.log, using a hard-coded Pinata access token."

Once registered, KuboShell checks Pinata for a command file named <MAC>.txt, and if the file exists, looks up the file’s IPFS identifier and downloads its contents through Pinata's public gateway. The downloaded content is executed via PowerShell in a hidden window. The results of the execution are saved in a file named "C:\Users\Public\<MAC>re.txt" and uploaded back to the server.

It's worth noting that the backdoor is not responsible for capturing the output. Rather, the results are returned only if the received command writes them to the text file. KuboShell then checks for a new command every 60 seconds.

Analysis indicates that KuboShell is primarily used to run basic reconnaissance commands and assess the compromised environment before downloading and executing a more capable backdoor, which includes the modular Homa Framework. This involves a three-stage process -

PowerShell stager, which contacts a hard-coded IP address ("185.205.187[.]109:8000") to fetch a PowerShell loader and execute it in memory

PowerShell loader, which decodes and launches a JavaScript backdoor

JavaScript Backdoor, which implements a continuous C2 loop to receive and execute PowerShell, SSH, and "cmd.exe" commands

It's suspected that the third-stage backdoor is used to execute additional modules, although the precise nature of those components is presently unknown.

"We assess that Homa's client is a JavaScript reimplementation of the older MuddyC2Go client, potentially allowing Volant Manticore to retain the more complex server-side component with minimal modifications, thereby reducing development time and resources," Check Point said.

The post-compromise framework has also been distributed via a macro-enabled Microsoft Word document called "MilitaryHeritageProposal.doc" that's believed to have targeted a Cypriot defense-related government entity. Enabling the content triggers the execution of a VBA backdoor that serves as a conduit for running follow-up payloads or commands using "cmd.exe."

"Volant Manticore shows how Iran's cyber ecosystem continues to reshape itself," Check Point concluded. "What appears to be a group of former MuddyWater operators now operates independently, pairing legacy MuddyWater tooling with new implants of their own while pursuing a regional focus that has until now drawn little attention."

"If MuddyC2Go is the latest MuddyWater framework Volant Manticore's operators had access to, the split may have happened around 2023 as MuddyWater replaced MuddyC2Go with DarkBeatC2 in late 2023.

items.title: How to compare MDR providers when every proposal looks promising
items.summary: Choosing a managed detection and response (MDR) provider means committing budget, connecting systems, and trusting another team to act when your organization is under pressure. Yet a proposal promising 24x7 coverage, expert analysts, and fast response can leave important questions unanswered. Which systems will actually be monitored? What will analysts investigate before contacting you? What happens when an incident needs more work? Before choosing a provider or renewing your current agreement, ask for evidence of how the service operates. Rapid7’s MDR Evaluation Scorecard gives you 18 checks to structure that conversation and record what still needs proving. Start with one investigation Ask a provider to walk you through a completed investigation, using an anonymized example where necessary. Follow the initial signal through the evidence considered, the analyst’s decision, and any response actions. Suppose suspicious activity involves an account with access to a critical business system. Can the provider show how the account’s permissions, the systems within reach, and known weaknesses influenced its investigation? Can it explain what it ruled out and why it escalated or contained the activity? This exercise helps you assess whether exposure context, intelligence, and customer telemetry work together. It also makes the division of work visible: what the provider investigated, what it decided, and what your team had to do next. Compare the service you would actually receive Use the same requirements for every provider, including your incumbent. Confirm the proposed service tier, supported integrations, response responsibilities, and total costs before comparing scores. Be specific about incident response. Establish who handles containment, forensics, eradication, and mitigation, which actions require your approval, and whether additional work changes the bill. A demonstration should be supported by written commitments about the service you would receive. Rapid7 MDR includes unlimited incident response, giving customers direct access to senior responders for digital forensics, eradication, and mitigation. When evaluating that commitment, ask us to explain the activities covered, how containment and remediation are coordinated, and which decisions remain with your team. Apply the same scrutiny to intelligence. Ask for an example showing how an emerging threat led to detection updates, hunting activity, or customer guidance. Rapid7’s emerging-threat response process connects research, detection engineering, product, and communications. The useful evaluation question is how that process changes the protection and advice customers receive. Look for improvement you can trace A detailed investigation record helps you understand what happened. Your next question should be what changed afterward. Look for recommendations that led to stronger controls, better detections, or closed coverage gaps. Ask how the provider reviews completed actions and recurring problems with your team. When comparing reporting, check whether you can trace those improvements alongside investigation volumes and response measures. Turn the answers into a decision The scorecard covers six areas: exposure-aware detection, intelligence, response ownership and cost, transparency, team expertise, and integration. Rate each capability against evidence, then record limitations, outstanding questions, and follow-up owners. The total helps organize your comparison, but essential requirements deserve individual attention. A strong overall score cannot compensate for a response capability your organization needs and the proposed service excludes. Download the MDR Evaluation Scorecard before your next provider review, shortlist meeting, or renewal discussion. Use it to make the evidence comparable and identify exactly what needs resolving before you commit.

The kernel-rt packages provide the Real Time Linux Kernel, which enables fine-tuning for systems with extremely high determinism requirements.

kernel: netfilter: nf_tables: prevent nf_skb_duplicated corruption (CVE-2024-49952)

kernel: nvmet-rdma: handle inline data with a nonzero offset (CVE-2026-72129)

kernel: Bluetooth: mgmt: fix UAF in pair command cancellation (CVE-2026-74510)

For more details about the security issue(s), including the impact, a CVSS score, acknowledgments, and other related information, refer to the CVE page(s) listed in the References section.

For details on how to apply this update, which includes the changes described in this advisory, refer to:

The system must be rebooted for this update to take effect.

Red Hat recommends treating all kernel errata as security-relevant. Given the kernel's fundamental role, any bug has a higher chance of impacting system security, even if that impact only becomes clear after a fix is published. Therefore, Red Hat prioritizes delivering fixes that improve our customers' overall security posture.

Because of this proactive approach, a patch may be associated with a CVE assignment at a future date. Retroactive CVE assignments are always documented in the corresponding errata and on Red Hat's CVE pages. We strongly advise against delaying updates, as doing so may leave your system exposed when protections are already available.

items.title: Recent Trends and Tactics of Agentic AI Attacks
items.summary: We tracked campaigns where attackers deployed autonomous AI agents to automate multi-platform intrusions, using standard tools while leaving distinct operational traces. The post Recent Trends and Tactics of Agentic AI Attacks appeared first on Unit 42 .
items.details:
We tracked campaigns where attackers deployed autonomous AI agents to automate multi-platform intrusions, using standard tools while leaving distinct operational traces.

Attackers are weaponizing autonomous AI agents in real-world campaigns, creating a risk that until recently has only been theoretical. Between July and September 2026, we identified and tracked more than 10 global campaigns in which different attackers deployed autonomous AI agents to enhance their attacks. These agentic AI attackers operated at machine speed, compressing the attack lifecycle from weeks or days into mere hours.

These campaigns targeted diverse sectors, including government, logistics, hospitality, manufacturing, agriculture and education. In every observed campaign the attackers gained their initial foothold through web shells that were deployed via vulnerable web applications.

The novelty of the observed agentic campaigns was not in their techniques, but in their speed and efficiency. Following the path of least resistance with familiar open-source tools and lightweight custom scripts, the AI-driven operators matched the tradecraft of proficient human attackers while operating at machine scale, at times executing hundreds of unique commands in just minutes.

However, using AI agents came at the expense of operational stealth. The agents left unmistakable behavioral fingerprints that revealed the involvement of non-human operators, including:

Chain-of-thought reasoning comments that appeared in shell commands

This article details the real-world scenarios that we observed, organized by the tactical patterns that define how agentic AI is being weaponized today.

Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed above through the following products and services:

Advanced URL Filtering , Advanced DNS Security and Advanced IP Defense

Next-Generation Firewall with the Advanced Threat Prevention

The Unit 42 AI Security Assessment service can help identify and mitigate complex AI-enabled risks.

Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI Defense is an offensive security service designed to assist organizations with continuously discovering hidden and unknown exposures in dynamic environments, validate real-world exploitability across attack paths through agentic testing and expert analysis, and provide prioritized remediation and virtual patching guidance to accelerate risk mitigation.

Organizations can access tailored adversary intelligence, direct analyst consultations, and specialized exposure tracking through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services and its Deep and Dark Web Service .

If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the Unit 42 Incident Response team .

An agentic AI attacker is an autonomous AI system — usually a large language model (LLM) with tool-calling capabilities — that independently plans, executes and adapts attack sequences without continuous human guidance remote.

Unlike chatbots that respond to individual prompts, agentic AI systems operate in a loop : they observe their environment, reason about what to do next, take action and then observe the results to inform their next step.

The weaponization of agentic AI represents an increased threat to security for several reasons:

Speed and scale: An agentic AI attacker operates at machine speed. In the campaigns we observed, AI agents executed hundreds of unique commands within minutes.

Lowered barrier to entry: Attackers can simply provide high-level guidance while the AI agent automates intricate technical phases. This includes complex actions such as compiling kernel exploits, navigating cross-platform lateral movement and systematically compromising cloud infrastructure.

Adaptive reasoning: Unlike script-based attacks that fail when they encounter unexpected conditions, agentic AI attackers employ reasoning to try alternative approaches when failures occur. We observed agents attempting five different privilege escalation techniques in sequence when earlier ones failed, compiling custom exploit code on-target when pre-built binaries didn’t work.

Cross-domain fluency: A single agentic AI attacker can operate across Linux, Windows, various cloud platforms, web applications, databases and network infrastructures. This breadth of expertise would typically require a team of specialists.

New challenges in threat attribution: Because AI agents generate unique, dynamic payloads on the fly without distinct behavioral fingerprints, attributing attacks to specific threat actors is increasingly difficult.

Our analysis of more than 10 campaigns observed between July and September 2026 indicates that the most successful intrusions consistently combined human oversight with AI agents in a unified operational model:

Human sets the objective: The human operator identifies a target and provides initial access — typically a web shell on a vulnerable web application. In some cases, the human operator executes the first assessment of the target.

AI agent takes over: The AI agent autonomously performs further reconnaissance, credential harvesting, privilege escalation and lateral movement.

AI agent reports back: The AI agent structures its findings using machine-readable output formatting and periodically checks in with orchestration APIs.

Human makes strategic decisions: The human operator reviews the AI agent’s findings and directs high-level strategy. This may include instructing the agent to target the payment system or establish persistence.

AI agent executes: The AI agent carries out the human’s strategic directives with tactical autonomy.

A comparative analysis of AI-assisted campaigns that we observed revealed several defining operational markers. These characteristics are strong indicators of an agentic attacker rather than a human operator:

One of the most pronounced characteristics of an attack performed by an AI operator is its ability to rapidly execute a high volume of commands.

In one attack we investigated, the AI attacker was active for only 140 minutes across two days. In this brief period of time, the attacker progressed from initial access via web shell, to performing reconnaissance and enumerating the victim’s cloud environment, website and databases. Throughout the attack, the AI agent executed about 800 unique commands at an inhuman pace.

items.title: ClamAV Vulnerabilities Affecting Cisco Products: November 2026
items.summary:
Multiple vulnerabilities in ClamAV could allow a remote attacker to bypass configured file and scan time limits and cause a denial of service (DoS) condition, interrupting scanning operations. For more information about these vulnerabilities, see the Details section of this advisory. For additional information on these vulnerabilities in ClamAV, see the ClamAV blog . Cisco has released software updates that address these vulnerabilities in affected Cisco platforms. There are no workarounds that address these vulnerabilities. Notes: The Security Impact Rating (SIR) for these vulnerabilities is High only for Windows-based platforms because those platforms run the ClamAV scanning process in a privileged security context. The platforms that are highly impacted include Cisco Secure Endpoint Connector for Windows. The SIR for these vulnerabilities is Medium on other platforms, including Linux and Mac platforms, because those platforms run the ClamAV scanning process in a lower-privileged security context. The affected platforms include Secure Endpoint Connector for Linux and Mac. Cisco Secure Endpoint Private Cloud itself is not impacted by these vulnerabilities. Instead, the Cisco Secure Endpoint Connector software is impacted. This advisory is available at the following link: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-clamav-multi-e93M3vdA
Security Impact Rating: High
CVE: CVE-2026-76411,CVE-2026-76414,CVE-2026-76415,CVE-2026-76416,CVE-2026-76417,CVE-2026-76421,CVE-2026-76422,CVE-2026-76430,CVE-2026-76515,CVE-2026-76516

Multiple vulnerabilities in ClamAV could allow a remote attacker to bypass configured file and scan time limits and cause a denial of service (DoS) condition, interrupting scanning operations.

For more information about these vulnerabilities, see the Details section of this advisory.

For additional information on these vulnerabilities in ClamAV, see the ClamAV blog .

Cisco has released software updates that address these vulnerabilities in affected Cisco platforms. There are no workarounds that address these vulnerabilities.

The Security Impact Rating (SIR) for these vulnerabilities is High only for Windows-based platforms because those platforms run the ClamAV scanning process in a privileged security context. The platforms that are highly impacted include Cisco Secure Endpoint Connector for Windows.

The SIR for these vulnerabilities is Medium on other platforms, including Linux and Mac platforms, because those platforms run the ClamAV scanning process in a lower-privileged security context. The affected platforms include Secure Endpoint Connector for Linux and Mac.

Cisco Secure Endpoint Private Cloud itself is not impacted by these vulnerabilities. Instead, the Cisco Secure Endpoint Connector software is impacted.

This advisory is available at the following link: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-clamav-multi-e93M3vdA

The following table lists Cisco products that are affected by the vulnerabilities that are described in this advisory. Customers should refer to the associated Cisco bug IDs for further details.

Cisco products may be impacted differently depending on implementation and usage of ClamAV. For information on the effects of these vulnerabilities on specific Cisco products, see the Details section of this advisory.

Only products listed in the Vulnerable Products section of this advisory are known to be affected by these vulnerabilities.

The vulnerabilities are not dependent on one another. Exploitation of one of the vulnerabilities is not required to exploit another vulnerability. In addition, a software release that is affected by one of the vulnerabilities may not be affected by the other vulnerabilities.

CVE-2026-76411: ClamAV Phishcheck Feature DoS Vulnerability

A vulnerability in the phishcheck functionality of ClamAV could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause a DoS condition on an affected device.

This vulnerability is due to improper allocation of memory when URLs are processed. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted URL to be processed by the software. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to cause the ClamAV scanning process to terminate, resulting in a DoS condition on the affected software.

Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability.

Bug ID(s): CSCwv98582 CVE ID: CVE-2026-76411 Security Impact Rating (SIR): High CVSS Base Score: 7.5 CVSS Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H

CVE-2026-76414: ClamAV Microsoft Compiled HTML Help File Infinite Loop Vulnerability

A vulnerability in Microsoft Compiled HTML Help (CHM) file scanning of ClamAV could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause a DoS condition on an affected device.

This vulnerability is due to a logic error when scanning a CHM file and following the internal file pointers. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted CHM file for scanning. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to cause the ClamAV decode process to terminate due to an infinite loop, resulting in a DoS condition on the affected software.

Bug ID(s): CSCwv99244 CVE ID: CVE-2026-76414 Security Impact Rating (SIR): High CVSS Base Score: 7.5 CVSS Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H

CVE-2026-76415: ClamAV Yoda's Crypter Portable Executable Unpacker Memory Read Underflow Vulnerability

A vulnerability in the Yoda's Crypter (yC) Portable Executable (PE) unpacker of ClamAV could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause a DoS condition on an affected device.

This vulnerability is due to lack of proper error checking for negative values when processing a PE file. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted PE file to be unpacked. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to cause the ClamAV scanning process to terminate, resulting in a DoS condition on the affected software.

Bug ID(s): CSCwv99214 CVE ID: CVE-2026-76415 Security Impact Rating (SIR): High CVSS Base Score: 7.5 CVSS Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H

CVE-2026-76416: ClamAV InstallShield File Parser Infinite Worker Loop Vulnerability

A vulnerability in the InstallShield file parser of ClamAV could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause a DoS condition on an affected device.

This vulnerability is due to incomplete error checking when the InstallShield file parser performs a scan. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted InstallShield file to be scanned. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to cause the ClamAV scanning process to terminate due to an infinite worker loop, resulting in a DoS condition on the affected software.

Bug ID(s): CSCwv99250 CVE ID: CVE-2026-76416 Security Impact Rating (SIR): High CVSS Base Score: 7.5 CVSS Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H

CVE-2026-76417: ClamAV Object Linking and Embedding Version 2 Memory Exhaustion Vulnerability

Red Hat recommends treating all kernel errata as security-relevant. items.details:
Broadcom patches 23 VMware flaws, including a critical vCenter authentication bypass that could allow unauthorized access to the system.

Broadcom has shipped patches to address 23 vulnerabilities impacting VMware ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, and Avi Load Balancer, including one critical bug that could be abused to bypass authentication.

The critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123903 , is rated 9.8 out of 10.0 on the CVSS scoring system. It resides in the VMware Directory Service ("vmdir").

"A malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system," Broadcom said in an advisory released today.

The company credited sglab of QiAnXin, Qi Qin (@LeoQ7_) of depthfirst, and VulTeam and XGTP from ThreatBook for independently reporting the flaw.

Also patched in vCenter are four high-severity flaws, including an arbitrary file write vulnerability while processing certain archives that could be exploited to achieve code execution on the appliance (CVE-2026-123904, CVSS score: 7.5).

The remaining three vulnerabilities relate to denial-of-service in the VMware Directory Service (CVE-2026-123905, CVE-2026-123906, and CVE-2026-123907, CVSS scores: 7.5).

The issues have been addressed in the following versions -

VMware Cloud Foundation and VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.x - Fixed in 9.1.2

VMware Cloud Foundation and VMware vSphere Foundation 9.0.x.x - Fixed in 9.0.2.0300

VMware vCenter 7.0 (Contact Broadcom Support, if on extended support contract)

VMware Telco Cloud Platform - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2)

VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2)

The fixes arrive days after Broadcom shipped updates for CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), another authentication bypass flaw impacting the VMware Directory Service that was exploited as a zero-day by a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group called Armory Castle. VMware has noted that CVE-2026-123903 is a distinct issue and is not related to CVE-2026-123890.

While Broadcom makes no mention of any of the newly disclosed flaws as being exploited in the wild, it's essential that customers apply the updates for optimal protection.

items.details:
Okta links an active vishing cluster previously associated with ShinyHunters to the INCEPTION leak site, but its operators remain unconfirmed.

A threat cluster previously assessed to be affiliated with the ShinyHunters extortion crew may have rebranded and continued operations under a new name called INCEPTION , according to Okta's Threat Intelligence team.

The cluster, dubbed O-UNC-053 , is characterized by the use of voice phishing (aka vishing) attacks to trick targets into entering credentials in phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA). Okta said it's been tracking the group since March 2026.

The identity and access management provider said targets of this cluster previously had stolen data published to the ShinyHunters data leak site (DLS). However, as of November 16, 2026, a new data leak site operating under the name INCEPTION has listed the data siphoned from O-UNC-053 targets.

"While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers resulting in data theft and extortion," Okta researchers Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

Social engineering and credential harvesting attacks mounted by O-UNC-053 have targeted a broad range of sectors, including technology, healthcare, biotechnology, financial services, insurance, entertainment, gaming, retail, transportation, hospitality, and legal.

Similar to O-UNC-066 and UNC6671 , the newly identified cluster also relies on a phishing kit to intercept authentication flows and capture a user's credentials and MFA codes. However, the kit is not designed to bypass phishing-resistant methods like passkeys and Okta FastPass.

"While interacting with targeted users on the phone, the operators socially engineer them into sharing factors like one-time passcodes and approving push notifications," Okta said. "If successful, the operators gain access to SaaS applications and exfiltrate sensitive data, which is often used to extort targets under the threat of releasing it on a data leak site."

Domains created by the group are registered through NiceNIC, Spaceship, Tucows, and NameSilo, with the domain names using the following patterns -

The use of "legal" themes in these attacks is said to have started in October 2026, and is often registered on or within a day of a campaign starting. Prior campaign waves have employed help desk-, support-, and claims-related themes for the registered domains.

These findings also dovetail with an alert from Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, which has warned of widespread vishing activity using legal-themed domains that either begin with "legal-" or end with "-legal" using the ".com" top-level domain.

More than 70 such domains have been observed since October 2026, it said, adding each domain is specifically created for an intended target operating in different industries, like cryptocurrency, financial services, healthcare, high technology, and hospitality, among others.

"Registered in rapid evening batches and shielded behind Cloudflare, these web-only domains deploy a filtered kit that delivers tailored content to intended victims while routing visitors it is not configured to attack to the targeted organization's legitimate Okta or NetIQ sign-in flow," ReversingLabs researcher Robert Simmons said .

Some of the confirmed domains linked to the activity are listed below -

The crux of the campaign is to tailor the landing page to the specific identity provider of the target, while filtering unwanted visitors and forwarding them to the organization's authentication infrastructure, such as Okta.

"Throughout our tracking of O-UNC-053 between March and September 2026, we observed the names of targeted entities appear on the ShinyHunters DLS between 1 and 28 days after the phishing infrastructure was registered," Okta noted.

However, it's unclear at this stage if the published data on the INCEPTION site is authentic and whether they are running the site themselves or are collaborating with another extortion gang. The exact nature of the relationship between ShinyHunters and O-UNC-053 is also unknown.

It's worth noting that the ShinyHunters data leak site went offline in late September 2026 following the arrest of three alleged members of the group, including a Canadian co-conspirator responsible for the breach of the FBIjobs.gov portal.

There is no evidence of data from O-UNC-053 targets being published on any data leak site from early September 2026 through October and early November 2026, until listings for multiple targets appeared on the INCEPTION site last week.

"This gap in publishing on any leak site followed by publishing on a new data leak site with a new brand is consistent with prior shifts from Com -affiliated actors," Okta said. "Regardless of the nature of the relationship with the INCEPTION DLS, O-UNC-053 remains active in conducting vishing attacks against targets in an effort to take over accounts, steal data, and extort targets."

In a post on their dark web site, INCEPTION has denied any affiliation with ShinyHunters, insisting that it operates independently with its own members and objectives.

"We are not ShinyHunters. We were never ShinyHunters. We are INCEPTION," the group said, adding "certain parties in the threat intelligence industry have been eager to give us a history we never asked for."

"We are also not copying anyone. If our methodology resembles what came before, it is because we took inspiration from operators who, whatever else may be said of them, understood that the weakest component of any secure system is a human being holding a phone. That is not theft of tradecraft. It is acknowledgment of a good idea -- the same way every group after LockBit used a leak site, and nobody called them LockBit."

When reached for comment regarding INCEPTION's latest claims, Okta told The Hacker that its "threat intelligence advisories are built on rigorous analysis of observed threat activity and documented operational patterns," adding "our priority is to shed light on the evolution of phishing campaigns and help o

(The story was updated after publication to include a statement posted by INCEPTION on its dark web site and a response from Okta.)

Red Hat Product Security has rated this update as having a security impact of Important. A Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) base score, which gives a detailed severity rating, is available for each vulnerability from the CVE link(s) in the References section.

LERC is an open-source image or raster format which supports rapid encoding and decoding for any pixel type (not just RGB or Byte). Users set the maximum compression error per pixel while encoding, so the precision of the original input image is preserved (within user defined error bounds).

items.title: Rapid7 Analysis: VMware vCenter SRP Authentication Bypass to Root (CVE-2026-123890)
items.details:
An unauthenticated attacker can retrieve the session key for an in-progress administrator login to VMware vCenter's directory service. The attacker then uses that key to complete the login without knowing the account's password. The vulnerable interface is exposed through DCE/RPC on TCP port 2012.

The issue, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 , combines a Secure Remote Password (SRP) session-key getter that is callable before authentication with an RPC context lookup that does not enforce ownership. The context handles use predictable UUIDv1 values. By creating two reference contexts around a pending login, an attacker can narrow the hidden login handle to a short timestamp window and ask the server for its key.

The attacker needs network access to TCP 2012 and the name of an existing SSO principal. Our PoC uses the default SSO administrator principal, [email protected] ; deployments using a different SSO domain need the corresponding account name. The attack does not depend on an existing authenticated connection or an administrator being online. The attacker initiates the login attempt in order to recover its session key.

The authenticated connection can call the directory database-copy interface. Its raw database contains the STS private signing key, allowing the attacker to sign administrator assertions that vCenter trusts. Our attack workflow used a forged assertion to create a local appliance superAdmin account, enable SSH and Bash, and execute commands as root through sudo. This final part requires access to the HTTPS API on TCP 443 and SSH on TCP 22, in addition to TCP 2012. It uses the administrative privileges obtained through the original bypass; no second vulnerability is needed once you have administrative RPC access.

The SRP RPC getter receives an SRP verifier at [A1], obtains its session key at [A2], and returns a copy at [A3]. It checks whether the verifier and key exist. It does not check whether the caller has authenticated, whether the caller owns the verifier, or whether the SRP client has supplied a valid password proof.

The value at [A1] is a server-side pointer that the RPC runtime resolves from the context handle supplied in the request. Each newly created verifier context receives its own UUID, so the attacker needs the handle for the specific pending login they want to complete. These context UUIDs identify individual verifier instances; the fixed interface UUIDs identify the available RPC interfaces.

UUIDv1 values contain a timestamp, clock sequence, and node identifier. The attacker creates a verifier immediately before starting the target login and another immediately afterward, obtaining both reference UUIDs without authenticating. On the tested service, the reference UUIDs share their clock sequence and node identifier. The attacker reuses those fields and searches the intervening timestamps for the pending login's live verifier, keeping the login connection open throughout the search.

The underlying SRP library exposes the authentication flag separately at [A4]. Its key getter at [A5] does not consult that flag. The server has already computed the shared key while generating its challenge, because it needs that key to verify the client's proof. Returning it at this stage gives the client the secret needed to produce that proof.

The RPC runtime takes the supplied UUID at [B1], searches a process-wide table at [B2], and returns the associated context at [B3]. There is no comparison with the requesting connection or its authenticated identity. Although context creation records a client for lifetime management, that client is not part of this lookup's authorization decision (hooray!!).

We confirmed the boundary directly: one anonymous RPC connection created an SRP verifier, and a second anonymous connection retrieved that verifier's key before any password proof was sent. The first connection's context handle was enough to make the second connection's request succeed.

The service registers the helper with a secure-interface flag and an authentication callback. On the tested TCP path, however, the RPC executor retrieves those registration values and dispatches the server stub without enforcing the callback. Other directory handlers perform their own access checks. The SRP key getter has no equivalent check, leaving it reachable before authentication.

The UUID timestamp generator reads the wall clock at [C1] and converts its microseconds into 100-nanosecond UUID ticks at [C2]. The resulting UUIDv1 handle also contains a clock sequence and node identifier. In our captures, those latter fields remain stable while newly created contexts advance through the timestamp space.

vmdir manages this SRP authentication exchange through the Generic Security Service API (GSS-API), which provides a common interface for authentication mechanisms. Starting the login creates an SRP verifier internally, but the login client does not receive its context handle.

An attacker can obtain reference handles by creating ordinary SRP verifiers through the helper interface. Creating one immediately before the GSS-API login and another immediately afterward bounds the timestamp of its hidden verifier. The shared node and clock-sequence fields then let the attacker construct candidate UUIDs within that interval.

The default search advances in increments of ten UUID ticks, matching the clock's microsecond resolution. The generator also supports uniqueness adjustments within a clock tick, so the PoC includes a one-tick search mode. Clock changes, concurrent activity, and the chosen search bounds can affect recovery; exhausting the window does not establish that a target is patched.

The service exposes two relevant RPC interfaces on port 2012:

SRP-authenticated bind, directory state, and database open/read/close

The helper's operation numbers are 0 for verifier creation, 1 for key retrieval, and 4 for deletion. GetState is operation 4 on the separate vmdirdbcp interface. The interface UUID is therefore part of identifying an operation; the operation number alone is ambiguous.

The client first creates a reference verifier, starts a separate SRP login as the target principal (e.g. [email protected] ), and creates the second reference verifier. It keeps the login connection open while querying candidate handles over another anonymous connection. These are all connections controlled by the attacker.

GSS does not return the handle for its own verifier. A reference verifier for the same principal has a different session key, so retrieving that reference key does not complete the pending GSS login. We need the key from the verifier associated with the login connection; the reference handles only narrow the search for it.

In the final standalone PoC test, the reference handles were:

The interval between the reference timestamps was 115,610 UUID ticks, or about 11.56 milliseconds. The search recovered the hidden handle shown above after 5,083 queries. Four workers issued the queries in that Python test, so the count includes requests that were already in flight when the match was found.

The SRP verifier helper returns the pending login's actual 20-byte session key. The attack does not need a weak password, a password hash from disk, or an invalid SRP public value.

Here, I is the requested principal, N and g are the SRP group parameters, s is the server's salt, and A and B are the public values exchanged during login. The server sends s alongside B in its initial SRP challenge, before the client supplies a password proof. The salt is public: a legitimate client uses it with the password to derive the values needed for authentication.

The client already has all of these inputs except K . Once the key getter supplies K , the client can calculate the normal client proof, M1 , and verify the server's response, HAMK .

The attack does not need a weak password, a password hash from disk, or an invalid SRP public value. Our client uses the valid public value A = 2 in the normal 2048-bit group. The reference verifiers use the cheaper 1024-bit group only to obtain the timing bounds.

The implementation hashes minimal big-endian integer representations. On the tested build, the returned B is 276 bytes because CSRP serializes k*v + g^b without first reducing the sum modulo N . Reducing or truncating that returned value while building the transcript produces the wrong proof.

The successful mechanism on this build is the legacy SRP OID 1.2.840.113554.1.2.10 . Its token framing also differs from a conventional GSS wrapper: the outer length covers the OID, with the SRP state token following it. The client carries the exchange in SPNEGO bind and ALTER_CONTEXT messages, using RPC packet privacy. Matching that framing is necessary to reach the vulnerable authentication flow.

items.details:
GitHub Actions attackers exploited SHA pinning trust gaps to disguise malicious commits, while new workflow lockfiles leave provenance risks unresolve

Pinning GitHub Actions to an exact version of their code, known as SHA pinning, has become the go-to defense against software supply chain attacks. Attackers have already found a way around it.

In March 2026, the hackers who hijacked Trivy, a widely used open-source security scanner, planted malicious code that looked like it came from GitHub's official checkout tool. They even labeled it a security fix. Teams pinned to it would have passed every check.

The trick works because GitHub lets copies of a project, called forks, share code with the original. In May, the same technique hit the popular actions-cool/issues-helper tool, stealing credentials from the pipelines that ran it.

The lesson: pinning guarantees the code won't change, but not who wrote it.

That gap is the focus of an upcoming webinar, GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning . If your team treats pinning as the finish line, save your seat to learn what it actually protects you from, and what it doesn't.

Pinning earned its reputation. When the tj-actions/changed-files compromise repointed tags to a malicious commit across more than 23,000 repositories in March 2025, teams that had pinned to SHAs were unaffected.

GitHub now lets administrators enforce pinning as an organization-wide policy, and few security teams argue against it.

📅 Save Your Spot: Learn Why “Best Practice” Won’t Stop the Next GitHub Actions Attack

Authorship: A SHA doesn't tell you who wrote the commit. Any fork commit can be pinned.

Project membership: Org-level enforcement checks that a reference is a 40-character SHA, not that the commit actually lives in the upstream project.

Runtime: A Docker-based action pinned to a SHA can still build its image at runtime, pulling in dependencies that were never frozen.

With agentic development pushing more code through CI than ever, each of those gaps gets exercised more often and reviewed less closely.

GitHub's 2026 Actions security roadmap, published March 26, put deterministic dependency locking front and center. Workflow lockfiles entered public preview on October 14 and became generally available on October 28, 2026. They tie every run to recorded commits for actions and their transitive dependencies, even if a tag moves later.

That's real progress. Locked commits must exist on a branch of the source repository, which blunts fork-only impostors. But GitHub's own changelog is clear that locking "does not determine whether the dependency itself is safe." Commit authorship and runtime builds remain open; immutable releases only help when maintainers opt in, and lockfiles aren't currently supported on GitHub Enterprise Server.

Not sure where your pipelines fall in that gap? Register for the webinar for a clear-eyed breakdown of what GitHub's roadmap fixes and what it still leaves to you.

Led by Erika Heidi , Staff Developer Relations Engineer at Chainguard , the session draws a hard line between immutability and provenance, and covers:

What org-level pin enforcement actually verifies, and the false confidence it can create

How impostor commits work, and why GitHub's repository network makes them possible

What GitHub's Actions roadmap addresses, and what it doesn't

Other ways to close the trust gap, including a curated catalog of vetted actions

Platform and DevOps engineers who own CI/CD, AppSec and DevSecOps teams writing pipeline policy, and security leaders who signed off on SHA pinning as "done." If your workflows pull in third-party actions, this session is for you.

Attackers have already shown they can disguise a malicious commit as a hardening fix. The next one won't announce itself either.

Register now for GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning , pick the session time that works for you, and find out what your pins aren't telling you.

items.title: RHSA-2026:102887: Important: cifs-utils security update
items.summary: An update for cifs-utils is now available for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10. Red Hat Product Security has rated this update as having a security impact of Important. A Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) base score, which gives a detailed severity rating, is available for each vulnerability from the CVE link(s) in the References section.
items.details:
An update for cifs-utils is now available for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.

Red Hat Product Security has rated this update as having a security impact of Important. A Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) base score, which gives a detailed severity rating, is available for each vulnerability from the CVE link(s) in the References section.

The SMB/CIFS protocol is a standard file sharing protocol widely deployed on Microsoft Windows machines. The cifs-utils packages contain tools for mounting shares on Linux using the SMB/CIFS protocol. The tools in this package work in conjunction with support in the kernel to allow one to mount a SMB/CIFS share onto a client and use it as if it were a standard Linux file system.

cifs-utils: mount.cifs credential-file option injection allows local privilege boundary bypass (CVE-2026-104715)

For more details about the security issue(s), including the impact, a CVSS score, acknowledgments, and other related information, refer to the CVE page(s) listed in the References section.

items.title: Google Researcher Shows How a Single Bit Change in .NET Files Bypassed Windows Code Integrity
items.summary: A quirk in how the .NET Framework loads a program file let a local attacker run untrusted code past two separate protections on Windows built to block it, Google Project Zero researcher James Forshaw showed in a write-up published yesterday.
